    Riemannian Optimization · Chapter 03

    Embedded geometry: first order

    Stable source-facing chapter environment inside the shared Samplinglib reader.

    Partially formalizedsource mapFull source closure not claimed
    Chapter goal

    From feasible directions to gradients

    Turn smooth embedded geometry into first-order optimization: identify feasible directions, differentiate an objective along them, and use the induced metric to represent its differential by a gradient.

    Mathematical knowledge map

    1. Feasible directions

      The tangent space describes first-order motion within the embedded manifold. Affine directions are K; for the unit sphere the actual inclusion differential maps Mathlib tangent directions onto the ambient plane x⊥.

    2. Differentiate along the space

      Local agreement of extensions gives the same derivative on a true feasible-curve velocity. The sphere adapter now composes the actual inclusion differential with the ambient derivative to construct the true restricted manifold differential. General embedded-manifold tangent/differential and representing-curve adapters remain separate.

    3. Represent by the metric

      For the induced pairing, the gradient is the unique ambient tangent vector representing the differential. The sphere adapter tests every ambient tangent direction through the exact range of the inclusion differential. Changing the metric requires a separate adapter; no default chart inner product is substituted.

    4. Project the ambient gradient

      Orthogonal projection removes the normal component without changing tangent pairings. The affine lemma supplies the linear restriction prerequisite; the sphere theorem constructs and uniquely characterizes the projection for the actual nonlinear sphere differential.

    Current boundary. The curve lemma closes the explicit extension-choice proof edge following Proposition3.35; affine restriction supplies a projection prerequisite; the sphere theorem closes the actual induced-gradient characterization for the unit sphere. General embedded-manifold tangent/differential and extension identification, representing-curve independence/linearity, global induced-metric smoothness and smooth gradient fields remain open. These are scoped partial advances, not completion of either proposition or Chapter3.

    Proposition 3.35 and its extension-independence consequence

    Nicolas Boumal. Samplinglib attributed restatement. The canonical normed-space lemma generalizes only the selected curve proof edge.

    2023 pre-publication edition, annotations through2026-10-08 · §3.4 Definition3.34/(3.27), equation(3.28), Proposition3.35 and following extension-choice verification; printed35–36/PDF51–52 · faithful paraphrase

    Complete source statement (Samplinglib restatement)

    Let M⊆E and M′⊆E′ be embedded submanifolds of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let F:M→M′ be smooth, and let F̄ be any smooth ambient neighborhood extension. For every x∈M, the manifold differential is DF(x)=D F̄(x)|_{TₓM}. Consequently it is linear, depends on a representing curve only through its base point and velocity, and is independent of the extension: any second extension F̂ gives D F̄(x)[v]=D F̂(x)[v] for v∈TₓM.

    • M and M′ are embedded submanifolds of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces; F:M→M′ is smooth.
    • F̄ and F̂ are smooth neighborhood extensions of the same F.
    • Each tangent v at x is represented by a smooth feasible curve c with c(0)=x and c′(0)=v.

    Source differential restriction

    \[DF(x)=D\bar F(x)|_{T_xM}.\]

    Selected extension-choice proof edge

    \[D\bar F(x)[v]=(\bar F\circ c)\prime(0)=(\widehat F\circ c)\prime(0)=D\widehat F(x)[v],\quad c(0)=x,\ c\prime(0)=v.\]

    Samplinglib mathematical lesson

    Why the derivative along a feasible curve ignores the extension

    AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Geometry.CurveExtension.fderiv_eq_on_curve_velocity · theorem · Teaching coverage

    Read this first

    Mathematical statement

    Let E and V be real normed spaces, s⊆E, and f,g:E→V. At x=c(t₀), suppose f and g are genuinely differentiable, c has actual velocity v, c(t) lies in s for all t sufficiently near t₀, and f=g locally relative to s at x. Then Df(x)[v]=Dg(x)[v].

    \[x=c(t_0),\quad c\prime(t_0)=v,\qquad Df(x)[v]=Dg(x)[v].\]
    Lean statement · fderiv_eq_on_curve_velocity

    DifferentiableAt certifies both ambient derivatives; HasDerivAt certifies the actual curve velocity. Eventually in 𝓝 means locally near t₀. EventuallyEq in 𝓝[s] x means equality on a relative neighborhood. E→V are total Lean function types, but only their local germs enter this proof.

    Braces mark parameters Lean can infer; square brackets request structures such as a measurable space or probability measure. Named hypotheses are mathematical premises, not facts established by this declaration. Section parameters are described in the mathematical hypotheses above; the module link retains their exact source context.

    Download module (.lean)
    theorem fderiv_eq_on_curve_velocity
    {s : Set E} {f g : E → F} {c : ℝ → E} {t₀ : ℝ} {v : E}
    (hf : DifferentiableAt ℝ f (c t₀))
    (hg : DifferentiableAt ℝ g (c t₀))
    (hc : HasDerivAt c v t₀)
    (hcs : ∀ᶠ t in 𝓝 t₀, c t ∈ s)
    (hfg : f =ᶠ[𝓝[s] (c t₀)] g) :
    fderiv ℝ f (c t₀) v = fderiv ℝ g (c t₀) v

    Exact module and namespace context

    Proof roadmap
    1. 1Pull the agreement back to the curve
    2. 2Differentiate each image curve
    3. 3Use locality and uniqueness
    Full assumptions and notation

    All objects and hypotheses

    • E and V are real normed spaces, possibly infinite-dimensional and incomplete. No chosen Riemannian metric, inner product, Riesz gradient, orthogonal projector or manifold structure is required. This generalizes the finite-dimensional Euclidean source proof ingredient.
    • Both ambient maps have genuine pointwise Fréchet derivatives at x. Smoothness of the source extensions implies this condition. fderiv is not used to manufacture a derivative when none exists.
    • c:ℝ→E has a genuine derivative v at t₀ and lies locally in s. Source smooth manifold curves satisfy these weaker local requirements.
    • The two ambient maps agree on some relative neighborhood of x in s. They need not agree in any open ambient neighborhood. Source neighborhood extensions of the same manifold map supply this equality locally.

    Mathematical proof

    1. Pull the agreement back to the curve

    A differentiable curve is continuous. Together with local feasibility, continuity sends sufficiently small parameter neighborhoods into relative neighborhoods of x in s. The two image curves therefore agree near t₀. This is a local argument: neither extension needs to agree off the feasible set.

    \[f(c(t))=g(c(t))\quad\text{for all }t\text{ sufficiently near }t_0.\]
    Corresponding Lean step
      have hcts : Tendsto c (𝓝 t₀) (𝓝[s] (c t₀)) :=
    tendsto_nhdsWithin_iff.mpr ⟨hc.continuousAt, hcs⟩
  have hcomp : (f ∘ c) =ᶠ[𝓝 t₀] (g ∘ c) := hfg.comp_tendsto hcts

    HasDerivAt.continuousAt and tendsto_nhdsWithin_iff construct the relative-neighborhood limit. Filter.EventuallyEq.comp_tendsto pulls back local equality.

    2. Differentiate each image curve

    Apply the actual chain rule to each genuinely differentiable ambient map and the actual curve derivative. Its velocity is the ambient derivative applied to v. This derives both image derivatives inside the proof.

    \[(f\circ c)\prime(t_0)=Df(x)[v],\qquad (g\circ c)\prime(t_0)=Dg(x)[v].\]
    Corresponding Lean step
      have hfc := hf.hasFDerivAt.comp_hasDerivAt t₀ hc
  have hgc := hg.hasFDerivAt.comp_hasDerivAt t₀ hc

    DifferentiableAt.hasFDerivAt gives a real derivative witness; HasFDerivAt.comp_hasDerivAt is the Fréchet/one-parameter chain rule.

    3. Use locality and uniqueness

    Locally equal image curves share their derivative at t₀. Transfer the first derivative witness to the second image curve; uniqueness then equates the two velocities. For every source tangent vector represented by a smooth feasible curve, this gives the extension-choice equality. The remaining manifold tangent adapter must be supplied separately.

    \[Df(x)[v]=(f\circ c)\prime(t_0)=(g\circ c)\prime(t_0)=Dg(x)[v].\]
    Corresponding Lean step
      exact (hfc.congr_of_eventuallyEq hcomp.symm).unique hgc

    HasDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq transfers the witness. HasDerivAt.unique compares two genuine derivatives of one image curve.

      Proposition 3.61 · ambient-to-tangent gradient projection

      Nicolas Boumal. ASTIS attributed restatement. Affine restriction is a prerequisite; sphere projection is a scoped nonlinear application. Neither completes the general embedded-manifold theorem.

      2023 pre-publication edition, annotations through 2026-10-08 · §3.8, Definition3.58 and equations3.36–3.38; Proposition3.61 (3.39), printed42–44 / PDF58–60 · faithful paraphrase

      Complete source statement (Samplinglib restatement)

      On a Riemannian submanifold of Euclidean space with the induced metric, the gradient of a smooth function is the tangent-space orthogonal projection of the ambient gradient of any smooth neighborhood extension.

      • Finite-dimensional Euclidean ambient space and embedded submanifold with induced Riemannian metric.
      • Smooth real-valued f on the manifold and a smooth extension to a neighborhood.

      Source projection formula

      \[\operatorname{grad}_Mf(x)=P_{T_xM}\operatorname{grad}_E\bar f(x).\]

      Read the formalized proofs

      Each statement and proof below has its own closed Lean disclosure. Samplinglib parents, Mathlib calls and external mathematical sources are distinguished in each proof.

      Samplinglib mathematical lesson

      Project the gradient when restricting to an affine subspace

      AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Geometry.AffineGradient.hasGradientAt_affine_restriction · theorem · Teaching coverage

      Read this first

      Mathematical statement

      Let E be a real Hilbert space and K a complete linear subspace with inherited metric. If f has genuine ambient gradient g at a+u, then the affine restriction F_a(v)=f(a+v), v∈K, has genuine gradient P_K g at u.

      \[F_a(v)=f(a+v),\qquad \nabla_KF_a(u)=P_K\nabla_Ef(a+u).\]
      Lean statement · hasGradientAt_affine_restriction

      K is a subtype with its own inherited inner product. HasGradientAt includes genuine differentiability. The result is typed in K; a is a point shift, not part of the gradient. Completeness supplies the Riesz gradient and orthogonal projector.

      Braces mark parameters Lean can infer; square brackets request structures such as a measurable space or probability measure. Named hypotheses are mathematical premises, not facts established by this declaration. Section parameters are described in the mathematical hypotheses above; the module link retains their exact source context.

      Download module (.lean)
      theorem hasGradientAt_affine_restriction
    (K : Submodule ℝ E) [CompleteSpace K]
    {f : E → ℝ} {a g : E} {u : K}
    (hf : HasGradientAt f g (a + (u : E))) :
    HasGradientAt (fun v : K => f (a + (v : E)))
      (K.orthogonalProjectionOnto g) u

      Exact module and namespace context

      Proof roadmap
      1. 1Differentiate the affine parameterization
      2. 2Apply the actual chain rule
      3. 3Remove the normal component and identify the gradient
      Full assumptions and notation

      All objects and hypotheses

      • E is a complete real inner-product space; K is a complete real linear subspace with the inherited inner product. These assumptions generalize the finite-dimensional Euclidean source.
      • f:E→ℝ, a,g:E and u∈K. The genuine ambient gradient g exists at a+u: HasGradientAt f g (a+u). No totalized derivative is used as a regularity witness.
      • The restriction is the literal map F_a:K→ℝ, v↦f(a+v). Its gradient is a direction in K, not the affine point a+P_K g.

      Mathematical proof

      1. Differentiate the affine parameterization

      For v in the direction space, the chart i_a(v)=a+v has derivative equal to the inclusion K↪E. The shift changes the evaluation point but contributes zero derivative.

      \[Di_a(u)[v]=v,\qquad i_a(u)=a+u.\]
      Corresponding Lean step
        have hchart : HasFDerivAt (fun v : K => a + (v : E)) K.subtypeL u := by
    convert (hasFDerivAt_const a u).add K.subtypeL.hasFDerivAt using 1 <;>
      first | rfl | simp only [zero_add]

      hchart: derivative of the constant plus the continuous linear inclusion.

      2. Apply the actual chain rule

      The ambient gradient represents Df(a+u). Composing with the chart derivative produces the restriction derivative for every v∈K; this derivative is proved rather than supplied.

      \[DF_a(u)[v]=Df(a+u)[v]=\langle g,v\rangle_E.\]
      Corresponding Lean step
        have hcomp := hf.hasFDerivAt.comp u hchart

      hf.hasFDerivAt.comp u hchart; the Riesz functional is InnerProductSpace.toDual.

      3. Remove the normal component and identify the gradient

      The residual g−P_K g is perpendicular to K. Therefore all tangent pairings agree. With the inherited metric the projected vector represents exactly the restriction derivative, which proves the genuine gradient assertion and hence its uniqueness through the existing gradient API.

      \[\langle g,v\rangle_E=\langle P_Kg,v\rangle_K\quad(v\in K),\qquad \nabla_KF_a(u)=P_Kg.\]
      Corresponding Lean step
        have hdual : (InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ E g).comp K.subtypeL =
      InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ K (K.orthogonalProjectionOnto g) := by
    ext v
    simp
  rw [hdual] at hcomp
  exact hasGradientAt_iff_hasFDerivAt.mpr hcomp

      hdual uses Submodule.inner_orthogonalProjectionOnto_eq_of_mem_right; hasGradientAt_iff_hasFDerivAt finishes.

      Lean verification

      The exact proof begins folded immediately after the mathematical argument; the statement is folded beside the claim above.

    HasGradientAt (fun v : K => f (a + (v : E)))
      (K.orthogonalProjectionOnto g) u := by
  have hchart : HasFDerivAt (fun v : K => a + (v : E)) K.subtypeL u := by
    convert (hasFDerivAt_const a u).add K.subtypeL.hasFDerivAt using 1 <;>

        Samplinglib mathematical lesson

        The induced gradient on the sphere is a projection

        AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Geometry.SphereGradient.sphere_gradient_characterization · theorem · Teaching coverage

        Read this first

        Mathematical statement

        Let E be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space of dimension n+1 and let x be on its unit sphere. If the ambient objective f has genuine gradient g at x, its restriction F to the sphere has a unique ambient tangent representative of its actual manifold differential. That representative is the orthogonal projection of g onto T=x⊥. The pairing uses the actual inclusion derivative Aₓ, so it specifies the induced metric rather than a default chart inner product.

        \[T=(\mathbb R x)^\perp,\quad A_x=D\iota(x),\quad F=f\circ\iota,\qquad DF(x)[w]=\langle A_xw,z\rangle_E\ \forall w\ \Longleftrightarrow\ z=P_Tg\quad(z\in T).\]
        Lean statement · sphere_gradient_characterization

        TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x is the actual Mathlib tangent type for the unit sphere. mvfderiv is the true vector/scalar-valued manifold differential. z is in the ambient orthogonal tangent subspace; all w are quantified. The conclusion is a characterization, so it supplies existence by setting z=P_Tg and uniqueness for any candidate.

        Braces mark parameters Lean can infer; square brackets request structures such as a measurable space or probability measure. Named hypotheses are mathematical premises, not facts established by this declaration. Section parameters are described in the mathematical hypotheses above; the module link retains their exact source context.

        Download module (.lean)
        theorem sphere_gradient_characterization
    (n : ℕ) [Fact (Module.finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]
    (x : sphere (0 : E) 1) {f : E → ℝ} {g : E}
    (hf : HasGradientAt f g (x : E)) :
    ∀ z : (ℝ ∙ (x : E))ᗮ,
      ((∀ w : TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x,
        mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => f (y : E)) x w =
          ⟪mvfderiv (𝓡 n) ((↑) : sphere (0 : E) 1 → E) x w, (z : E)⟫_ℝ) ↔
        z = (ℝ ∙ (x : E))ᗮ.orthogonalProjectionOnto g)

        Exact module and namespace context

        Proof roadmap
        1. 1Identify actual tangent directions
        2. 2Differentiate the actual restricted objective
        3. 3Remove the normal component
        4. 4Prove uniqueness on the whole tangent plane
        Full assumptions and notation

        All objects and hypotheses

        • E is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space; dim E=n+1 and n may be0. Finite dimension supplies completeness and closedness of the tangent subspace, so no extra analytical premise is added.
        • x lies on the unit sphere, and f:E→ℝ has a genuine gradient g at x. Source smoothness implies this pointwise HasGradientAt witness; the theorem explicitly allows weaker pointwise regularity.
        • F is the literal restriction y↦f(y). Source maps on an ambient open neighborhood can be represented by their local germs, but arbitrary smooth extension construction is not proved.
        • Mathlib chart tangent directions are sent into the ambient tangent plane by the actual derivative Aₓ of the sphere inclusion. Its exact range is proved by Mathlib and used internally, not assumed. The induced pairing is ⟨Aₓw,Aₓw′⟩E; no default chart norm/inner product is identified with it.

        Mathematical proof

        1. Identify actual tangent directions

        The sphere inclusion is differentiable. Its differential Aₓ has range exactly the ambient plane T orthogonal to x. Thus every actual chart tangent direction maps into T, and every vector in T has a preimage. The companion injectivity theorem makes the pullback of the ambient pairing positive definite; the present ambient-representative proof uses the exact range.

        \[\operatorname{range} A_x=T=(\mathbb R x)^\perp,\qquad \langle w,w\prime\rangle_x=\langle A_xw,A_xw\prime\rangle_E.\]
        Corresponding Lean step
          let K := (ℝ ∙ (x : E))ᗮ
  let A := mvfderiv (𝓡 n) ((↑) : sphere (0 : E) 1 → E) x
  have hA : A.range = K := range_mvfderiv_subtypeVal x
  have hco := (contMDiff_coe_sphere (n := n) (m := 1) x).mdifferentiableAt one_ne_zero

        contMDiff_coe_sphere gives actual differentiability; range_mvfderiv_subtypeVal supplies both directions of the tangent identification. injective_mvfderiv_subtypeVal_sphere is background for interpreting the induced metric, not a call in this proof.

        2. Differentiate the actual restricted objective

        Apply the manifold chain rule to F=f∘ι. The ambient gradient is a genuine derivative witness, so evaluating the result at w gives the ambient pairing with its true direction Aₓw. Explicit vector-space tangent identification reconciles target types; it changes neither the differential nor the metric.

        \[DF(x)[w]=Df(x)[A_xw]=\langle g,A_xw\rangle_E=\langle A_xw,g\rangle_E.\]
        Corresponding Lean step
          have hd : ∀ w : TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x,
      mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => f (y : E)) x w =
        ⟪A w, g⟫_ℝ := by
    intro w
    have hchain := mvfderiv_comp x hf.differentiableAt.mdifferentiableAt hco
    change mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (f ∘ ((↑) : sphere (0 : E) 1 → E)) x w = _
    rw [hchain]
    convert! (hf.fderiv_apply (y := A w)) using 1 <;>
      simp [A, mvfderiv, NormedSpace.fromTangentSpace, real_inner_comm] <;> rfl

        mvfderiv_comp and HasGradientAt.fderiv_apply provide the mathematical equalities. NormedSpace.fromTangentSpace is the explicit trivial-vector-space tangent identification; convert/rfl only reconciles its identity map.

        3. Remove the normal component

        For each w, Aₓw belongs to T. Orthogonal projection changes g only by a vector perpendicular to T, so it preserves this pairing. The projected vector is already typed in T, furnishing an actual candidate gradient representative.

        \[\langle A_xw,g\rangle_E=\langle A_xw,P_Tg\rangle_E.\]
        Corresponding Lean step
          have hp : ∀ w : TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x,
      mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => f (y : E)) x w =
        ⟪A w, (K.orthogonalProjectionOnto g : E)⟫_ℝ := by
    intro w
    have hw : A w ∈ K := hA ▸ (show A w ∈ A.range from ⟨w, rfl⟩)
    rw [hd w]
    exact (K.inner_orthogonalProjectionOnto_eq_of_mem_left ⟨A w, hw⟩ g).symm

        Submodule.inner_orthogonalProjectionOnto_eq_of_mem_left applies to the proved tangent membership. No differential equality for the candidate is supplied as a premise.

        4. Prove uniqueness on the whole tangent plane

        Suppose a tangent candidate z has the same differential pairings for every chart direction. Given any v in T, use the exact-range identity to choose w with Aₓw=v. The two candidates pair equally with every v in T. Nondegeneracy of its inherited inner product gives z=P_Tg. Conversely, the projected candidate satisfies all pairings by the preceding step.

        \[\forall v\in T,\ \langle v,z\rangle_E=\langle v,P_Tg\rangle_E\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=P_Tg.\]
        Corresponding Lean step
          intro z
  constructor
  · intro hz
    apply ext_inner_left ℝ
    intro v
    have hv : (v : E) ∈ A.range := hA.symm ▸ v.property
    obtain ⟨w, hw⟩ := hv
    change ⟪(v : E), (z : E)⟫_ℝ = ⟪(v : E), (K.orthogonalProjectionOnto g : E)⟫_ℝ
    rw [← hw]
    exact (hz w).symm.trans (hp w)
  · rintro rfl
    exact hp

        Range surjectivity supplies each test direction; ext_inner_left proves uniqueness in the ambient tangent subspace. This constructs the candidate and proves its characterization before defining any chosen gradient object.

    (n : ℕ) [Fact (Module.finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]
    (x : sphere (0 : E) 1) {f : E → ℝ} {g : E}
    (hf : HasGradientAt f g (x : E)) :

        mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => f (y : E)) x w =

        z = (ℝ ∙ (x : E))ᗮ.orthogonalProjectionOnto g) := by
  let K := (ℝ ∙ (x : E))ᗮ
  let A := mvfderiv (𝓡 n) ((↑) : sphere (0 : E) 1 → E) x
  have hA : A.range = K := range_mvfderiv_subtypeVal x
  have hco := (contMDiff_coe_sphere (n := n) (m := 1) x).mdifferentiableAt one_ne_zero
  have hd : ∀ w : TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x,
      mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => f (y : E)) x w =
        ⟪A w, g⟫_ℝ := by
    intro w
    have hchain := mvfderiv_comp x hf.differentiableAt.mdifferentiableAt hco
    change mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (f ∘ ((↑) : sphere (0 : E) 1 → E)) x w = _
    rw [hchain]
    convert! (hf.fderiv_apply (y := A w)) using 1 <;>
      simp [A, mvfderiv, NormedSpace.fromTangentSpace, real_inner_comm] <;> rfl
  have hp : ∀ w : TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x,
      mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => f (y : E)) x w =
        ⟪A w, (K.orthogonalProjectionOnto g : E)⟫_ℝ := by
    intro w
    have hw : A w ∈ K := hA ▸ (show A w ∈ A.range from ⟨w, rfl⟩)
    rw [hd w]
    exact (K.inner_orthogonalProjectionOnto_eq_of_mem_left ⟨A w, hw⟩ g).symm
  intro z
  constructor
  · intro hz
    apply ext_inner_left ℝ
    intro v
    have hv : (v : E) ∈ A.range := hA.symm ▸ v.property
    obtain ⟨w, hw⟩ := hv

          Example 3.62 · Rayleigh gradient and critical eigenvectors

          Nicolas Boumal. ASTIS-authored restatement of the sphere application and its two stationarity directions; no source text/PDF redistributed.

          2023 pre-publication edition, annotations through 2026-10-08 · Boumal2023 pre-publication annotations through2026-10-08, §3.8 Example3.62 and(3.40), printed44/PDF60; §3.4 Example3.36 printed36/PDF52; induced metric/gradient conventions §§3.7–3.8 · faithful paraphrase

          Complete source statement (Samplinglib restatement)

          For a real symmetric matrix A, let F(x)=xᵀAx on the unit sphere with the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product. The chosen smooth ambient quadratic extension has gradient2Ax. The tangent projector sends u to u−⟨x,u⟩x, so the sphere gradient is2(Ax−⟨x,Ax⟩x). Its vanishing is equivalent to Ax=⟨x,Ax⟩x; thus the stationary unit vectors are exactly eigenvectors of A, and every unit eigenvector is stationary.

          • Finite-dimensional real Euclidean space, real symmetric matrix A and a unit vector x.
          • Unit sphere with the metric induced by the ambient inner product; F(x)=xᵀAx, the sphere restriction of the smooth quadratic extension.

          Unit tangent projector and gradient

          \[P_xu=u-\langle x,u\rangle x,\qquad \operatorname{grad}_S F(x)=2(Ax-\langle x,Ax\rangle x).\]

          Both directions of stationarity

          \[\operatorname{grad}_S F(x)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ Ax=\langle x,Ax\rangle x\ \Longleftrightarrow\ x\text{ is a unit eigenvector of }A.\]

          Read the formalized proofs

          Each statement and proof below has its own closed Lean disclosure. Samplinglib parents, Mathlib calls and external mathematical sources are distinguished in each proof.

          Samplinglib mathematical lesson

          Rayleigh objective: remove the radial part of 2Ax

          AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Geometry.SphereRayleigh.sphere_rayleigh_characterization · theorem · Teaching coverage

          Read this first

          Mathematical statement

          For a symmetric linear operator A on a finite-dimensional real Euclidean space, let F(x)=⟨x,Ax⟩ on the unit sphere. With its induced metric, the unique ambient tangent vector representing the genuine sphere differential is Gₓ=2(Ax−⟨x,Ax⟩x). More explicitly, every z in x⊥ represents that differential against every actual tangent direction exactly when z=Gₓ.

          \[\begin{gathered}F(x)=\langle x,Ax\rangle,\quad T_xS=x^\perp,\quad J_x=D\iota(x),\\ DF(x)[w]=\langle J_xw,z\rangle\ \forall w\ \Longleftrightarrow\ z=G_x\quad(z\in x^\perp),\\ G_x=2(Ax-\langle x,Ax\rangle x).\end{gathered}\]
          Lean statement · sphere_rayleigh_characterization

          All source data are quantified. z is typed in the ambient tangent plane x⊥, w in the actual Mathlib TangentSpace. The inclusion differential Jₓ transports w into the ambient space for the exact induced pairing. The iff yields the explicit unique representative; it is not a definition of a new gradient field.

Named hypotheses are mathematical premises, not facts established by this declaration.           theorem sphere_rayleigh_characterization
    (n : ℕ) [Fact (Module.finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]
    (A : E →L[ℝ] E) (hA : A.IsSymmetric) (x : sphere (0 : E) 1) :
    ∀ z : (ℝ ∙ (x : E))ᗮ,
      ((∀ w : TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x,
        mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => ⟪(y : E), A (y : E)⟫_ℝ) x w =
          ⟪mvfderiv (𝓡 n) ((↑) : sphere (0 : E) 1 → E) x w, (z : E)⟫_ℝ) ↔
        (z : E) = (2 : ℝ) • (A (x : E) - ⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ • (x : E)))

          Exact module and namespace context

          Proof roadmap
          1. 1Differentiate the symmetric quadratic
          2. 2Project onto the actual tangent plane
          3. 3Use the induced differential characterization
          Full assumptions and notation

          All objects and hypotheses

          • E is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space of dimension n+1. In orthonormal coordinates A is the source real symmetric matrix; its continuous-linear-map representation adds no regularity assumption in finite dimension.
          • A is symmetric, not necessarily positive, positive definite or invertible. x has norm one. Nonzeroness of x and the Rayleigh eigenvalue identity are derived internally, not added hypotheses.
          • The objective is the literal sphere restriction F(x)=⟨x,Ax⟩ of the smooth quadratic q(y)=⟨y,Ay⟩. The ambient quotient is defined only for y≠0; its equality with this restriction uses ‖x‖=1. No derivative of an off-domain totalized quotient is used.
          • The metric is the ambient-induced one. The actual inclusion derivative Jₓ maps abstract chart directions into x⊥. Pairings with Jₓw express this induced metric explicitly; no default chart inner product is identified with it.
          • n may be zero. The claims are pointwise, with every x and every tangent test direction quantified. They neither construct a global gradient-field object nor claim a convergence or extremal-eigenvalue theorem.

          Mathematical proof

          1. Differentiate the symmetric quadratic

          Expand q(x+tv). Symmetry makes the two first-order cross terms equal, giving Dq(x)[v]=2⟨Ax,v⟩ and hence the genuine ambient gradient 2Ax. The implementation reuses Mathlib’s derivative, proves that its quadratic is literally q, and identifies its linear functional with the gradient dual. No gradient witness is supplied by the reader.

          \[q(x+tv)=q(x)+2t\langle Ax,v\rangle+t^2q(v),\qquad Dq(x)[v]=2\langle Ax,v\rangle,\quad \nabla q(x)=2Ax.\]
          Corresponding Lean step
            have hx : ‖(x : E)‖ = 1 := mem_sphere_zero_iff_norm.mp x.property
  have hg : HasGradientAt (fun y : E => ⟪y, A y⟫_ℝ) ((2 : ℝ) • A (x : E)) (x : E) := by
    apply hasGradientAt_iff_hasFDerivAt.mpr
    have hraw := (hA.hasStrictFDerivAt_reApplyInnerSelf (x : E)).hasFDerivAt
    have hfun : (fun y : E => ⟪y, A y⟫_ℝ) = A.reApplyInnerSelf := by
      funext y
      simp [ContinuousLinearMap.reApplyInnerSelf_apply, real_inner_comm]
    have hlin : toDual ℝ E ((2 : ℝ) • A (x : E)) =
        (2 : ℕ) • innerSL ℝ (A (x : E)) := by
      ext v
      simp [toDual_apply_apply, two_smul]
    rw [hfun, hlin]
    exact hraw

          The strict derivative API writes its coefficient as natural-number addition twice; two_smul identifies it with multiplication by the real scalar2. This is an API adapter, not a change of normalization.

          2. Project onto the actual tangent plane

          Because x is a unit vector, the projection onto its normal line sends u to ⟨x,u⟩x. Subtracting this normal component gives the projection onto x⊥. Apply this to 2Ax and use bilinearity to obtain the displayed vector Gₓ. In particular Gₓ is tangent: ⟨x,Gₓ⟩=2(⟨x,Ax⟩−⟨x,Ax⟩‖x‖²)=0.

          \[P_{x^\perp}u=u-\langle x,u\rangle x,\qquad P_{x^\perp}(2Ax)=2(Ax-\langle x,Ax\rangle x).\]
          Corresponding Lean step
            let K := (ℝ ∙ (x : E))ᗮ
  have hproj (u : E) : (K.orthogonalProjectionOnto u : E) =
      u - ⟪(x : E), u⟫_ℝ • (x : E) := by
    change (ℝ ∙ (x : E))ᗮ.starProjection u = _
    rw [Submodule.starProjection_orthogonal_val,
      Submodule.starProjection_unit_singleton ℝ hx]
  have hp : (K.orthogonalProjectionOnto ((2 : ℝ) • A (x : E)) : E) =
      (2 : ℝ) • (A (x : E) - ⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ • (x : E)) := by
    rw [hproj]
    simp [inner_smul_right, smul_sub, smul_smul]

          Submodule.starProjection_orthogonal_val and starProjection_unit_singleton supply the exact projection formula. The local hproj holds for every ambient u and covers source equation3.40; no duplicate public projection lemma is introduced.

          3. Use the induced differential characterization

          The existing genuine-sphere theorem applies to the actual ambient gradient just proved. The inclusion chain rule and its exact tangent range are already established in that parent: the restricted differential pairs with a tangent candidate precisely when it is the orthogonal projection. Replacing that projection by Gₓ gives the claimed formula and uniqueness. Existence uses the projected vector in x⊥, not an assumed solution.

          \[\begin{gathered}DF(x)[w]=Dq(x)[J_xw]=\langle J_xw,2Ax\rangle=\langle J_xw,G_x\rangle,\\ z\text{ represents }DF(x)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ z=G_x.\end{gathered}\]
          Corresponding Lean step
            intro z
  rw [SphereGradient.sphere_gradient_characterization n x hg z]
  constructor
  · intro hz
    exact (congrArg (fun v : K => (v : E)) hz).trans hp
  · intro hz
    apply Subtype.ext
    exact hz.trans hp.symm

          The canonical SphereGradient.sphere_gradient_characterization supplies the true nonlinear differential and uniqueness. Subtype.ext and congrArg only move the already tangent projection between its subtype and ambient representation.

          Samplinglib mathematical lesson

          Sphere stationary points are exactly unit eigenvectors

          AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Geometry.SphereRayleigh.sphere_rayleigh_stationary_iff · theorem · Teaching coverage

          Read this first

          Mathematical statement

          For the same symmetric quadratic on the induced unit sphere, the genuine manifold differential at x is zero exactly when Ax=⟨x,Ax⟩x, and exactly when x is an eigenvector of A. If Ax=μx, the unit norm forces μ=⟨x,Ax⟩. Zero or negative eigenvalues are allowed.

          \[\begin{gathered}DF(x)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ Ax=\langle x,Ax\rangle x\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists\mu\in\mathbb R:\ Ax=\mu x,\ x\ne0,\\ Ax=\mu x\Rightarrow\mu=\langle x,Ax\rangle.\end{gathered}\]
          Lean statement · sphere_rayleigh_stationary_iff

          The first conjunct identifies a zero continuous-linear-map differential with the Rayleigh equation. The second conjunct identifies it with an existential actual Module.End.HasEigenvector. All x on the unit sphere are quantified, and no nonzero-eigenvalue premise is present.

          Braces mark parameters Lean can infer; square brackets request structures such as a measurable space or probability measure. Named hypotheses are mathematical premises, not facts established by this declaration. Section parameters are described in the mathematical hypotheses above; the module link retains their exact source context.

          Download module (.lean)
          theorem sphere_rayleigh_stationary_iff
    (n : ℕ) [Fact (Module.finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]
    (A : E →L[ℝ] E) (hA : A.IsSymmetric) (x : sphere (0 : E) 1) :
    (mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => ⟪(y : E), A (y : E)⟫_ℝ) x = 0 ↔
      A (x : E) = ⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ • (x : E)) ∧
    (mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => ⟪(y : E), A (y : E)⟫_ℝ) x = 0 ↔
      ∃ μ : ℝ, Module.End.HasEigenvector A.toLinearMap μ (x : E))

          Exact module and namespace context

          Proof roadmap
          1. 1Turn zero differential into zero projected gradient
          2. 2A stationary unit vector is an eigenvector
          3. 3Every unit eigenvector is stationary
          Full assumptions and notation

          All objects and hypotheses

          • E is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space of dimension n+1. In orthonormal coordinates A is the source real symmetric matrix; its continuous-linear-map representation adds no regularity assumption in finite dimension.
          • A is symmetric, not necessarily positive, positive definite or invertible. x has norm one. Nonzeroness of x and the Rayleigh eigenvalue identity are derived internally, not added hypotheses.
          • The objective is the literal sphere restriction F(x)=⟨x,Ax⟩ of the smooth quadratic q(y)=⟨y,Ay⟩. The ambient quotient is defined only for y≠0; its equality with this restriction uses ‖x‖=1. No derivative of an off-domain totalized quotient is used.
          • The metric is the ambient-induced one. The actual inclusion derivative Jₓ maps abstract chart directions into x⊥. Pairings with Jₓw express this induced metric explicitly; no default chart inner product is identified with it.
          • n may be zero. The claims are pointwise, with every x and every tangent test direction quantified. They neither construct a global gradient-field object nor claim a convergence or extremal-eigenvalue theorem.

          Mathematical proof

          1. Turn zero differential into zero projected gradient

          A continuous linear differential is zero exactly when it vanishes on every tangent direction. The first theorem at the candidate z=0 says that these vanishing pairings hold precisely when Gₓ=0. This explicitly implements the source-derived bridge from differential stationarity to induced-gradient stationarity. Cancel the nonzero real scalar2 and rearrange the difference.

          \[DF(x)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ DF(x)[w]=0\ \forall w\ \Longleftrightarrow\ 0=2(Ax-\langle x,Ax\rangle x)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ Ax=\langle x,Ax\rangle x.\]
          Corresponding Lean step
            have hx : ‖(x : E)‖ = 1 := mem_sphere_zero_iff_norm.mp x.property
  have hxne : (x : E) ≠ 0 := by
    intro hz
    simp [hz] at hx
  have hzero := sphere_rayleigh_characterization n A hA x 0
  have hd :
      mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => ⟪(y : E), A (y : E)⟫_ℝ) x = 0 ↔
        A (x : E) = ⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ • (x : E) := by
    have he :
        mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => ⟪(y : E), A (y : E)⟫_ℝ) x = 0 ↔
          ∀ w : TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x,
            mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => ⟪(y : E), A (y : E)⟫_ℝ) x w = 0 := by
      constructor
      · intro h w
        rw [h]
        rfl
      · intro h
        ext w
        exact h w
    rw [he]
    have hs : (0 : E) = (2 : ℝ) •
        (A (x : E) - ⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ • (x : E)) ↔
          A (x : E) = ⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ • (x : E) := by
      rw [eq_comm, smul_eq_zero, sub_eq_zero]
      simp
    have hpair :
        (∀ w : TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x,
          mvfderiv (𝓡 n) (fun y : sphere (0 : E) 1 => ⟪(y : E), A (y : E)⟫_ℝ) x w = 0) ↔
          (0 : E) = (2 : ℝ) • (A (x : E) - ⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ • (x : E)) := by
      simpa only [Submodule.coe_zero, inner_zero_right] using hzero
    exact hpair.trans hs

          The proof uses extensionality of the actual differential, not an arbitrary supplied pairing identity. The characterization tests every chart direction through the canonical induced pairing. Norm one gives x≠0 internally.

          2. A stationary unit vector is an eigenvector

          The preceding equality puts x in the eigenspace with eigenvalue ⟨x,Ax⟩. Unit membership proves x≠0, so this is genuine eigenvectorhood in the library sense rather than the equation alone, which would also hold at zero.

          \[Ax=\langle x,Ax\rangle x,\quad\|x\|=1\Rightarrow x\ne0,\qquad x\in E_{\langle x,Ax\rangle}(A)\setminus\{0\}.\]
          Corresponding Lean step
            refine ⟨hd, ?_⟩
  constructor
  · intro h
    exact ⟨⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ,
      Module.End.mem_eigenspace_iff.mpr (hd.mp h), hxne⟩

          Module.End.mem_eigenspace_iff supplies eigenspace membership; HasEigenvector includes the proved nonzeroness. No spectral existence theorem or positivity assumption is needed.

          3. Every unit eigenvector is stationary

          Conversely, suppose Ax=μx. Pair with x to get ⟨x,Ax⟩=μ‖x‖²=μ. Thus the eigenvector equation is exactly the Rayleigh-coefficient equation, and the first equivalence gives DF(x)=0. This proves the converse for any real eigenvalue, including zero and negative values.

          \[\langle x,Ax\rangle=\langle x,\mu x\rangle=\mu\|x\|^2=\mu,\qquad Ax=\langle x,Ax\rangle x\Rightarrow DF(x)=0.\]
          Corresponding Lean step
            · rintro ⟨μ, hμ⟩
    have hAx : A (x : E) = μ • (x : E) := hμ.apply_eq_smul
    have hcoef : ⟪(x : E), A (x : E)⟫_ℝ = μ := by
      rw [hAx, inner_smul_right]
      simp [hx]
    apply hd.mpr
    rw [hcoef]
    exact hAx

          HasEigenvector.apply_eq_smul gives the actual eigenvalue equation. The coefficient identity uses the source unit norm; it is not added as a theorem hypothesis.

            The projected Hessian trace removes the radial term

            Original Samplinglib library statement. External textbook links in the lesson provide mathematical context; this is not claimed to be a verbatim numbered textbook theorem.

            Samplinglib shared mathematical supplements, Lean 4.33.0 · Original Samplinglib supplement: The projected Hessian trace removes the radial term. Exact assumptions and formula below. (historical source) · licensed original

            Complete source statement and conditions

            Let $w$ be a unit vector in a real Euclidean space with finite coordinate set $I$, let $(e_j)_{j\in I}$ be its coordinate basis, and let $f$ be a real ambient test function. Write $p_j=e_j-w_jw$. The trace of the ambient second Fréchet derivative evaluated on the pairs $(p_j,p_j)$ equals the ambient Laplacian minus the radial Hessian entry.

            • The finite coordinate set has decidable equality. The point $w$ has Euclidean norm one.
            • For an analytic interpretation of the Hessian, take a twice continuously differentiable ambient test near $w$. The Lean equality itself is algebraic in the totalized Fréchet derivatives and has no smoothness premise.

            Claim

            \[\sum_{j\in I}D^2f(w)[p_j,p_j]=\Delta_{\mathbb R^I}f(w)-D^2f(w)[w,w].\]

            Read the formalized proofs

            Each statement and proof below has its own closed Lean disclosure. Samplinglib parents, Mathlib calls and external mathematical sources are distinguished in each proof.

            Samplinglib mathematical lesson

            The projected Hessian trace removes the radial term

            Read this first

            Mathematical statement

            Let $w$ be a unit vector in a real Euclidean space with finite coordinate set $I$, let $(e_j)_{j\in I}$ be its coordinate basis, and let $f$ be a real ambient test function. Write $p_j=e_j-w_jw$. The trace of the ambient second Fréchet derivative evaluated on the pairs $(p_j,p_j)$ equals the ambient Laplacian minus the radial Hessian entry.

            \[\sum_{j\in I}D^2f(w)[p_j,p_j]=\Delta_{\mathbb R^I}f(w)-D^2f(w)[w,w].\]
            Lean statement · sum_hessian_projectedNoiseColumn

            The equality uses Mathlib's ambient Laplacian and the iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated twice in the radial direction.

    (∑ j : I, fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ f) w (projectedNoiseColumn j w)

      (Δ f) w - fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ f) w w w

            • For an analytic interpretation of the Hessian, take a twice continuously differentiable ambient test near $w$. The Lean equality itself is algebraic in the totalized Fréchet derivatives and has no smoothness premise.

            Mathematical proof

            Open a step to read its argument and formula.

            1. Expand the projected arguments

            Bilinearity gives two mixed radial terms and one term with two radial arguments for each coordinate.

            \[D^2 f[p_j,p_j]=D^2 f[e_j,e_j]-w_jD^2 f[e_j,w]-w_jD^2 f[w,e_j]+w_j^2D^2 f[w,w].\]

        EuclideanSpace.basisFun I ℝ = e from rfl, map_sub, map_smul,
      sub_apply, smul_apply, smul_eq_mul]
    ring
            2. Sum the radial contributions

            The coordinate expansion of $w$ makes each mixed sum equal to the radial Hessian entry. The unit norm makes the squared-coordinate sum one. The remaining diagonal sum is Mathlib's ambient Laplacian.

            \[\sum_j w_je_j=w,\qquad \sum_jw_j^2=1.\]

            The algebraic sphere-generator identity

            Original Samplinglib library statement. External textbook links in the lesson provide mathematical context; this is not claimed to be a verbatim numbered textbook theorem.

            Samplinglib shared mathematical supplements, Lean 4.33.0 · Original Samplinglib supplement: The algebraic sphere-generator identity. Exact assumptions and formula below. (historical source) · licensed original

            Complete source statement and conditions

            Fix a unit vector \(w\in\mathbb R^I\), a real function \(f\), an ambient vector \(u\), and \(\lambda\ge0\). Interpret \(Df\) and \(D^2f\) as the total Fréchet-derivative operators used in Lean. With projected columns \(p_j=e_j-w_jw\), the displayed algebraic equality holds. For a C² ambient test near the unit sphere, it is the usual identity for the Itô generator with noise columns \(\sqrt{2\lambda}\,p_j\) and radial drift \(-\lambda(d-1)w\), where \(d=|I|\).

            • The coordinate set is finite with decidable equality, $\|w\|=1$, and $\lambda\ge 0$.
            • The vector \(u\) is arbitrary. No smoothness hypothesis is needed for the total-derivative algebra equality. The interpretation as a classical generator requires a C² ambient test; when \(u\) is also tangent, its first-order term is the directional derivative of the restricted test.
            • The operators are total: Lean assigns zero to a Fréchet derivative where differentiability fails. The classical derivative interpretation is only asserted under the smooth-test qualification above.

            Claim

            \[Df(w)[-u-\lambda(d-1)w]+\frac12\sum_j D^2f(w)[\sqrt{2\lambda}\,p_j,\sqrt{2\lambda}\,p_j]=-Df(w)[u]+\lambda\Delta_{S^{d-1}}^{\rm ext} f(w).\]

            Read the formalized proofs

            Each statement and proof below has its own closed Lean disclosure. Samplinglib parents, Mathlib calls and external mathematical sources are distinguished in each proof.

            The algebraic sphere-generator identity

            Mathematical statement

            Fix a unit vector \(w\in\mathbb R^I\), a real function \(f\), an ambient vector \(u\), and \(\lambda\ge0\). Interpret \(Df\) and \(D^2f\) as the total Fréchet-derivative operators used in Lean. With projected columns \(p_j=e_j-w_jw\), the displayed algebraic equality holds. For a C² ambient test near the unit sphere, it is the usual identity for the Itô generator with noise columns \(\sqrt{2\lambda}\,p_j\) and radial drift \(-\lambda(d-1)w\), where \(d=|I|\).

            \[Df(w)[-u-\lambda(d-1)w]+\frac12\sum_j D^2f(w)[\sqrt{2\lambda}\,p_j,\sqrt{2\lambda}\,p_j]=-Df(w)[u]+\lambda\Delta_{S^{d-1}}^{\rm ext} f(w).\]

            The noise amplitude and inward radial drift are explicit. The dimension factor is the natural subtraction $|I|-1$ cast to the reals.

            theorem ito_generator_eq_sphereLaplacian
    (f : E → ℝ) {w : E} (hw : ‖w‖ = 1) (u : E) {temperature : ℝ}
    (hTemperature : 0 ≤ temperature) :
    let σ := fun j : I => Real.sqrt (2 * temperature) • projectedNoiseColumn j w
    let b := -u - (temperature * ((Fintype.card I - 1 : ℕ) : ℝ)) • w
    fderiv ℝ f w b +
      (1 / 2 : ℝ) * (∑ j : I, fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ f) w (σ j) (σ j)) =
      -fderiv ℝ f w u + temperature * sphereLaplacian f w

            Full assumptions and notation

            All objects and hypotheses

            • The coordinate set is finite with decidable equality, $\|w\|=1$, and $\lambda\ge 0$.
            • The vector \(u\) is arbitrary. No smoothness hypothesis is needed for the total-derivative algebra equality. The interpretation as a classical generator requires a C² ambient test; when \(u\) is also tangent, its first-order term is the directional derivative of the restricted test.
            • The operators are total: Lean assigns zero to a Fréchet derivative where differentiability fails. The classical derivative interpretation is only asserted under the smooth-test qualification above.

            Mathematical proof

            Open a step to read its argument and formula.

            1. Remove the noise amplitude from the trace

            The Hessian is bilinear and the square root is taken of a nonnegative number. Squaring the amplitude and multiplying by one half gives the temperature.

            \[\frac12(\sqrt{2\lambda})^2=\lambda.\]
            Corresponding Lean step
              intro σ b
  have hScale (j : I) :
      fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ f) w (σ j) (σ j) = (2 * temperature) *
        fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ f) w (projectedNoiseColumn j w) (projectedNoiseColumn j w) := by
    simp only [σ, map_smul, smul_apply, smul_eq_mul, ← mul_assoc,
      ← pow_two, Real.sq_sqrt (by positivity : 0 ≤ 2 * temperature)]
            2. Combine the radial drift and Hessian

            The projected trace removes one radial Hessian entry. The radial drift gives the first-derivative term with factor $d-1$.

            \[\Delta_{S^{d-1}}^{\rm ext} f(w)=\Delta_{\mathbb R^I}f(w)-D^2f(w)[w,w]-(d-1)Df(w)[w].\]
            Corresponding Lean step
              simp_rw [hScale, ← Finset.mul_sum, sum_hessian_projectedNoiseColumn f hw]
  simp only [b, map_sub, map_neg, map_smul, smul_eq_mul, sphereLaplacian]
  ring

              Samplinglib mathematical lesson

              A Hilbert feature potential has a controlled tangent Riesz field

              Read this first

              Mathematical statement

              Let E,H be complete real inner-product normed spaces. Let F:E→H be a map, and let each D(w):E→H be a continuous real linear map satisfying the actual ambient identity DF(w)=D(w) for every w. Suppose M₁,M₂≥0, ‖D(w)‖op≤M₁ on the closed unit ball, and ‖D(w)−D(u)‖op≤M₂‖w−u‖ there. For r∈H define V_r(w)=2⟨r,F(w)⟩ and G_r(w)=2(D(w)*r−⟨D(w)*r,w⟩w), where * is the Hilbert adjoint. At every ambient w, V_r has derivative 2⟨D(w)*r,·⟩. At every unit w, G_r(w) is tangent, satisfies ⟨G_r(w),v⟩=2⟨r,D(w)v⟩ for every v perpendicular to w, and has norm at most 2M₁‖r‖. For all r,q and unit w,u, its joint increment is bounded by 2M₁‖r−q‖+2(M₂+2M₁)‖q‖‖w−u‖.

              \[G_r(w)=2P_wD(w)^*r,\quad P_wz=z-\langle z,w\rangle w,\quad \|G_r(w)-G_q(u)\|\le2M_1\|r-q\|+2(M_2+2M_1)\|q\|\|w-u\|.\]

Suppose M₁,M₂≥0, ‖D(w)‖op≤M₁ on the closed unit ball, and ‖D(w)−D(u)‖op≤M₂‖w−u‖ there. For r∈H define V_r(w)=2⟨r,F(w)⟩ and G_r(w)=2(D(w)*r−⟨D(w)*r,w⟩w), where * is the Hilbert adjoint. At every ambient w, V_r has derivative 2⟨D(w)*r,·⟩. At every unit w, G_r(w) is tangent, satisfies ⟨G_r(w),v⟩=2⟨r,D(w)v⟩ for every v perpendicular to w, and has norm at most 2M₁‖r‖. For all r,q and unit w,u, its joint increment is bounded by 2M₁‖r−q‖+2(M₂+2M₁)‖q‖‖w−u‖.

              theorem quadratic_feature_potential_tangent_gradient
    {E H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [CompleteSpace E]
    [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H] [CompleteSpace H]
    (F : E → H) (D : E → E →L[ℝ] H)
    (hF : ∀ w, HasFDerivAt F (D w) w)
    (M₁ M₂ : ℝ) (hM₁ : 0 ≤ M₁) (hM₂ : 0 ≤ M₂)
    (hBound : ∀ w : E, ‖w‖ ≤ 1 → ‖D w‖ ≤ M₁)
    (hLip : ∀ w u : E, ‖w‖ ≤ 1 → ‖u‖ ≤ 1 → ‖D w-D u‖ ≤ M₂*‖w-u‖) :
    let V : H → E → ℝ := fun r w => 2 * ⟪r,F w⟫_ℝ
    let G : H → E → E := fun r w =>
      (2 : ℝ) • ((D w).adjoint r - ⟪(D w).adjoint r,w⟫_ℝ • w)
    (∀ r w, HasFDerivAt (V r) ((2 : ℝ) • innerSL ℝ ((D w).adjoint r)) w) ∧
    (∀ r w, ‖w‖ = 1 →
      ⟪w,G r w⟫_ℝ = 0 ∧
      (∀ v, ⟪w,v⟫_ℝ = 0 → ⟪G r w,v⟫_ℝ = 2 * ⟪r,D w v⟫_ℝ) ∧
      ‖G r w‖ ≤ 2 * M₁ * ‖r‖) ∧
    ∀ r q w u, ‖w‖ = 1 → ‖u‖ = 1 →
      ‖G r w-G q u‖ ≤ 2 * M₁ * ‖r-q‖ +
        2 * (M₂+2*M₁) * ‖q‖ * ‖w-u‖

              All objects and hypotheses

              • E,H are complete real inner-product normed spaces. F and D have the explicit actual full ambient Fréchet derivative relation.
              • M₁,M₂ are nonnegative; uniform derivative and operator Lipschitz bounds are explicit inputs on the closed unit ball. The tangent and joint field bounds require unit endpoint weights.

              Mathematical proof

              Open a step to read its argument and formula.

              1. Control the orthogonal projection

              For unit w, expand the squared norm of P_wz. Subtracting a nonnegative squared normal component proves contraction.

              \[\|P_wz\|^2=\|z\|^2-\langle z,w\rangle^2\le\|z\|^2.\]
              Corresponding Lean step
              private theorem P_norm_le {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    (w z : E) (hw : ‖w‖ = 1) : ‖P w z‖ ≤ ‖z‖ := by
  have hsq : ‖P w z‖^2 = ‖z‖^2 - ⟪z,w⟫_ℝ^2 := by
    simp only [P,norm_sub_sq_real,inner_smul_right,norm_smul,hw,mul_one,
      Real.norm_eq_abs,sq_abs]
    ring
  nlinarith [sq_nonneg ⟪z,w⟫_ℝ,norm_nonneg (P w z),norm_nonneg z]

Local names retain their surrounding theorem context; the complete theorem and exact module context are folded below. These excerpts are presentation, not extra theorem premises.

              2. Control projection movement

              Rewrite the projection difference into one change of vector direction and one change of its inner product. Cauchy–Schwarz and unit norms bound both terms.

              \[(P_w-P_u)z=\langle z,u\rangle(u-w)+\langle z,u-w\rangle w,\qquad \|(P_w-P_u)z\|\le2\|z\|\|w-u\|.\]
              Corresponding Lean step
              private theorem P_point_lip {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    (w u z : E) (hw : ‖w‖ = 1) (hu : ‖u‖ = 1) :
    ‖P w z-P u z‖ ≤ 2 * ‖z‖ * ‖w-u‖ := by
  have he : P w z-P u z = ⟪z,u⟫_ℝ • (u-w) + ⟪z,u-w⟫_ℝ • w := by
    simp only [P,inner_sub_right,smul_sub,sub_smul]
    abel
  rw [he]
  calc
    ‖⟪z,u⟫_ℝ • (u-w) + ⟪z,u-w⟫_ℝ • w‖ ≤
        ‖⟪z,u⟫_ℝ • (u-w)‖ + ‖⟪z,u-w⟫_ℝ • w‖ := norm_add_le _ _
    _ = ‖⟪z,u⟫_ℝ‖ * ‖u-w‖ + ‖⟪z,u-w⟫_ℝ‖ * ‖w‖ := by simp only [norm_smul]
    _ ≤ (‖z‖*‖u‖)*‖u-w‖ + (‖z‖*‖u-w‖)*‖w‖ := by
      gcongr <;> exact norm_inner_le_norm _ _
    _ = 2 * ‖z‖ * ‖w-u‖ := by rw [hw,hu,norm_sub_rev u w];ring

              3. Differentiate the scalar potential

              The chain rule for the bounded residual functional and the adjoint identity give the full ambient derivative. Projecting its representing vector removes only the normal part, which pairs to zero against every tangent direction.

              \[DV_r(w)v=2\langle r,D(w)v\rangle=2\langle D(w)^*r,v\rangle,\quad \langle w,G_r(w)\rangle=0.\]
              Corresponding Lean step

        sub_zero,ContinuousLinearMap.adjoint_inner_left]

              4. Bound the tangent field

              Adjoints preserve operator norms; the projection is contractive. Multiplication by two gives the asserted residual-dependent bound.

              \[\|G_r(w)\|\le2\|D(w)^*r\|\le2M_1\|r\|.\]

              5. Separate residual and location changes

              At a fixed w use linearity in r. For the fixed q location change, split the derivative-adjoint increment and the projection increment; combine the previous estimates.

              \[G_r(w)-G_q(u)=2P_wD(w)^*(r-q)+2P_w(D(w)^*-D(u)^*)q+2(P_w-P_u)D(u)^*q.\]

        add_le_add (P_norm_le _ _ hw) (P_point_lip _ _ _ hw hu)

  · intro r q w u hw hu

                Complete source statement and conditions

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure, let \(\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\), and let \(S=\{w\in E:\|w\|=1\}\). Let \(P\) be a probability measure on \(E\times\mathbb R\) whose first marginal is \(\gamma\). Fix a real polynomial \(p\), and assume the actual response \((x,y)\mapsto y\) belongs to \(H=L^2(P;\mathbb R)\). Define the literal feature and directional derivative by \(f_w(x,y)=p(\langle w,x\rangle)\) and \(df_{w,v}(x,y)=p^{\prime}(\langle w,x\rangle)\langle v,x\rangle\). All these functions belong to \(H\). There exist one family of continuous linear maps \(D(w):E\to H\) and positive constants \(M_1,M_2\), chosen before every parameter law and every subsequent evaluation point, with the following properties. Writing \(F(w)=[f_w]\), we have \(D(w)v=[df_{w,v}]\) and \(F\) has Fréchet derivative \(D(w)\) at every ambient \(w\). The displayed operator bounds hold on the closed unit ball. For every probability \(\rho\) on \(S\), all scalar sections defining the predictor are integrable, \(F|_S\) is Bochner integrable, and the predictor composed with the first-coordinate map belongs to \(H\), with class equal to its Bochner mean \(m_\rho\). The literal scalar potential has an integrable defining integrand at every ambient \(w\); it equals \(2\langle m_\rho-\ell,F(w)\rangle_H\) and has actual ambient gradient \(2D(w)^*(m_\rho-\ell)\) there. On the unit sphere, subtracting the normal component gives the final displayed projection formula. The same \(D,M_1,M_2\) is used throughout.

                • \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel measurable structure. Completeness follows from finite dimension. No positive-dimension or nonempty-sphere hypothesis is imposed.
                • \(E\times\mathbb R\) has its product measurable structure; \(P\) is a probability measure and \(P\circ\mathrm{fst}^{-1}=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\), the centered Gaussian with identity covariance.
                • \(p\in\mathbb R[X]\) is any finite polynomial. No coefficient normalization, degree bound or parity condition is assumed.
                • The actual response \((x,y)\mapsto y\) is square-integrable under \(P\). Independence of response and input is not required.
                • \(S\) has its subtype Borel structure. Every parameter law \(\rho\) is a probability on \(S\). Ambient derivative and potential statements range over all \(w,v\in E\); the operator bounds are restricted to the closed unit ball and the projection identity to \(w\in S\).
                • The feature and directional-derivative membership witnesses, \(D\), and \(M_1,M_2>0\) are conclusions, selected after \(E,P,p\) and the input hypotheses but before every \(\rho,w,u,v\). No law-dependent re-choice is made. No prescribed numerical or dimension-free bounds are claimed.

                Actual feature, mean, potential and gradient representation

                \[\begin{gathered}F(w)=[p(\langle w,x\rangle)]_P,\quad \ell=[y]_P,\quad D(w)v=[p^{\prime}(\langle w,x\rangle)\langle v,x\rangle]_P,\\ \mathrm dF(w)=D(w),\qquad \|D(w)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M_1\quad(\|w\|\le1),\\ \|D(w)-D(u)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M_2\|w-u\|\quad(\|w\|,\|u\|\le1),\\ a_\rho(x)=\int_Sp(\langle u,x\rangle)\,d\rho(u),\quad m_\rho=\int_S F(u)\,d\rho(u)=[a_\rho\circ\mathrm{fst}]_P,\\ V_\rho(w)=2\int_{E\times\mathbb R}(a_\rho(x)-y)p(\langle w,x\rangle)\,dP=2\langle m_\rho-\ell,F(w)\rangle_H,\\ \nabla V_\rho(w)=2D(w)^*(m_\rho-\ell)\quad(w\in E),\\ G_\rho(w):=\nabla V_\rho(w)-\langle\nabla V_\rho(w),w\rangle w\\ =2\bigl(D(w)^*(m_\rho-\ell)-\langle D(w)^*(m_\rho-\ell),w\rangle w\bigr)\quad(w\in S).\end{gathered}\]

                Mathematical statement

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure, let \(\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\), and let \(S=\{w\in E:\|w\|=1\}\). Let \(P\) be a probability measure on \(E\times\mathbb R\) whose first marginal is \(\gamma\). Fix a real polynomial \(p\), and assume the actual response \((x,y)\mapsto y\) belongs to \(H=L^2(P;\mathbb R)\). Define the literal feature and directional derivative by \(f_w(x,y)=p(\langle w,x\rangle)\) and \(df_{w,v}(x,y)=p^{\prime}(\langle w,x\rangle)\langle v,x\rangle\). All these functions belong to \(H\). There exist one family of continuous linear maps \(D(w):E\to H\) and positive constants \(M_1,M_2\), chosen before every parameter law and every subsequent evaluation point, with the following properties. Writing \(F(w)=[f_w]\), we have \(D(w)v=[df_{w,v}]\) and \(F\) has Fréchet derivative \(D(w)\) at every ambient \(w\). The displayed operator bounds hold on the closed unit ball. For every probability \(\rho\) on \(S\), all scalar sections defining the predictor are integrable, \(F|_S\) is Bochner integrable, and the predictor composed with the first-coordinate map belongs to \(H\), with class equal to its Bochner mean \(m_\rho\). The literal scalar potential has an integrable defining integrand at every ambient \(w\); it equals \(2\langle m_\rho-\ell,F(w)\rangle_H\) and has actual ambient gradient \(2D(w)^*(m_\rho-\ell)\) there.                 Exact module and namespace context

                This gives the actual feature, mean and gradient identities used by the following transport estimate. Proof strategy: Use the Gaussian L² derivative and its uniform bounds; Pull the feature and derivative into the joint law; Identify the actual predictor class with the Bochner mean; Recover the literal potential from the residual class; Use the adjoint to identify the ambient gradient; Substitute the gradient into the sphere projection.

                Full assumptions and notation

                All objects and hypotheses

                • \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel measurable structure. Completeness follows from finite dimension. No positive-dimension or nonempty-sphere hypothesis is imposed.
                • \(E\times\mathbb R\) has its product measurable structure; \(P\) is a probability measure and \(P\circ\mathrm{fst}^{-1}=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\), the centered Gaussian with identity covariance.
                • \(p\in\mathbb R[X]\) is any finite polynomial. No coefficient normalization, degree bound or parity condition is assumed.
                • The actual response \((x,y)\mapsto y\) is square-integrable under \(P\). Independence of response and input is not required.
                • \(S\) has its subtype Borel structure. Every parameter law \(\rho\) is a probability on \(S\). Ambient derivative and potential statements range over all \(w,v\in E\); the operator bounds are restricted to the closed unit ball and the projection identity to \(w\in S\).
                • The feature and directional-derivative membership witnesses, \(D\), and \(M_1,M_2>0\) are conclusions, selected after \(E,P,p\) and the input hypotheses but before every \(\rho,w,u,v\). No law-dependent re-choice is made. No prescribed numerical or dimension-free bounds are claimed.
                • \([h]_P\) denotes the actual \(L^2(P)\) equivalence class of a square-integrable scalar function. A class identity gives equality of representatives \(P\)-almost everywhere, not pointwise on the data space.
                • \(m_\rho\) is the Bochner integral in \(H\). The scalar potential identity and its gradient formula hold pointwise at every ambient weight, with scalar integrability proved as part of the result.
                • \(D(w)^*:H\to E\) is the Hilbert adjoint. The projection \(z\mapsto z-\langle z,w\rangle w\) is the orthogonal tangent projection when \(\|w\|=1\).

                Mathematical proof

                Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                1. Use the Gaussian L² derivative and its uniform bounds

                In \(H_0=L^2(\gamma)\), the existing polynomial-feature theorem supplies the classes \(\Phi(w)=[p(\langle w,\cdot\rangle)]_\gamma\), their actual derivative \(D_0(w)\), and positive bounds \(M_1,M_2\) on the closed unit ball. Its directional formula identifies the derivative class explicitly. These facts are outputs of that parent, so no derivative witness is assumed here.

                \[D_0(w)v=[p^{\prime}(\langle w,x\rangle)\langle v,x\rangle]_\gamma,\quad \mathrm d\Phi(w)=D_0(w),\quad \|D_0(w)\|\le M_1,\quad \|D_0(w)-D_0(u)\|\le M_2\|w-u\|.\]

    AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Probability.GaussianPolynomialDifferentiation.actual_gaussian_polynomial_ridge_L2_derivative_bounds (E := E) p

                Literal excerpt from the compiled candidate module. Local notation and earlier derived facts are available in the folded complete proof.

                2. Pull the feature and derivative into the joint law

                The first-marginal identity makes \(\mathrm{fst}\) measure preserving. Pullback gives a linear isometry \(J:H_0\to H\). Set \(F=J\Phi\) and \(D(w)=J\circ D_0(w)\). Pullback preserves the literal feature and directional-derivative classes. The chain rule gives the derivative of \(F\), and the isometry preserves the same operator bounds, with no use of response/input independence.

                \[J[h]_\gamma=[h\circ\mathrm{fst}]_P,\quad \|Jh\|_H=\|h\|_{H_0},\quad D(w)v=[df_{w,v}]_P,\quad \mathrm dF(w)=D(w).\]

                  have hmarg : MeasurePreserving (Prod.fst : E × ℝ → E) P (stdGaussian E) :=
    ⟨measurable_fst,hGaussian⟩
  let J : Lp ℝ 2 (stdGaussian E) →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Lp ℝ 2 P :=
    Lp.compMeasurePreservingₗᵢ ℝ Prod.fst hmarg
  let T : Lp ℝ 2 (stdGaussian E) →L[ℝ] Lp ℝ 2 P := J.toContinuousLinearMap
  let hfP : ∀ w : E, MemLp (fun z : E × ℝ => p.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ) 2 P :=
    fun w => (hf w).comp_measurePreserving hmarg
  let hdfP : ∀ w v : E,
      MemLp (fun z : E × ℝ => p.derivative.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ * ⟪v,z.1⟫_ℝ) 2 P :=
    fun w v => (hdf w v).comp_measurePreserving hmarg
  let F : E → Lp ℝ 2 P := fun w => (hfP w).toLp (fun z => p.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ)
  let DP : E → E →L[ℝ] Lp ℝ 2 P := fun w => T.comp (D w)
  have hDP (w v : E) : DP w v =
      (hdfP w v).toLp (fun z => p.derivative.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ * ⟪v,z.1⟫_ℝ) := by
    change T (D w v) = _
    rw [hD w v]
    rfl
  have hFeq (w : E) : F w = T ((hf w).toLp (fun x => p.eval ⟪w,x⟫_ℝ)) := rfl
  have hFP (w : E) : HasFDerivAt F (DP w) w := by
    have he : F = fun u => T ((hf u).toLp (fun x => p.eval ⟪u,x⟫_ℝ)) := funext hFeq
    rw [he]
    exact T.hasFDerivAt.comp w (hDiff w)
  have hPB (w : E) (hw : ‖w‖ ≤ 1) : ‖DP w‖ ≤ M₁ := by
    apply ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_le_bound _ hM₁.le
    intro v
    change ‖J (D w v)‖ ≤ M₁*‖v‖
    rw [J.norm_map]
    exact ((D w).le_opNorm v).trans (mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right (hBound w hw) (norm_nonneg v))
  have hPL (w u : E) (hw : ‖w‖ ≤ 1) (hu : ‖u‖ ≤ 1) :
      ‖DP w-DP u‖ ≤ M₂*‖w-u‖ := by
    apply ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_le_bound _ (mul_nonneg hM₂.le (norm_nonneg _))
    intro v
    change ‖T (D w v)-T (D u v)‖ ≤ (M₂*‖w-u‖)*‖v‖
    rw [← map_sub]
    change ‖J ((D w-D u) v)‖ ≤ (M₂*‖w-u‖)*‖v‖
    rw [J.norm_map]
    exact ((D w-D u).le_opNorm v).trans
      (mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right (hLip u w hu hw) (norm_nonneg v))

                3. Identify the actual predictor class with the Bochner mean

                The Gaussian parameter-average theorem proves scalar-section and Bochner integrability and identifies the predictor class in \(H_0\). Pull this class through \(J\) and commute the continuous linear map with the Bochner integral. This proves integrability of \(F|_S\) and identifies \(m_\rho\) with the actual predictor class in \(H\).

                \[[a_\rho\circ\mathrm{fst}]_P=J[a_\rho]_\gamma=J\!\left(\int_S\Phi(u)\,d\rho(u)\right)=\int_SF(u)\,d\rho(u)=m_\rho.\]

                4. Recover the literal potential from the residual class

                The class \(m_\rho-\ell\) has representative \(a_\rho(x)-y\) almost everywhere. Both this residual and the feature belong to \(L^2(P)\); Cauchy–Schwarz makes their product integrable. The \(L^2\) inner-product formula therefore turns the literal scalar potential into the displayed inner product for every ambient \(w\). The equality is a function identity in the weight variable.

                \[(m_\rho-\ell)(x,y)=a_\rho(x)-y\quad P\text{-a.e.},\qquad V_\rho(w)=2\int(a_\rho(x)-y)p(\langle w,x\rangle)\,dP=2\langle m_\rho-\ell,F(w)\rangle_H.\]

    rw [← hident]
    exact hpred.coeFn_toLp

    rw [hs,hm,hy]

    change F w z = p.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ at hw
    simp only [Real.inner_apply,hr,hw]

      (hdfP w v).toLp (fun z => p.derivative.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ * ⟪v,z.1⟫_ℝ) := by
    change T (D w v) = _
    rw [hD w v]
    rfl
  have hFeq (w : E) : F w = T ((hf w).toLp (fun x => p.eval ⟪w,x⟫_ℝ)) := rfl
  have hFP (w : E) : HasFDerivAt F (DP w) w := by
    have he : F = fun u => T ((hf u).toLp (fun x => p.eval ⟪u,x⟫_ℝ)) := funext hFeq
    rw [he]
    exact T.hasFDerivAt.comp w (hDiff w)
  have hPB (w : E) (hw : ‖w‖ ≤ 1) : ‖DP w‖ ≤ M₁ := by
    apply ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_le_bound _ hM₁.le
    intro v
    change ‖J (D w v)‖ ≤ M₁*‖v‖
    rw [J.norm_map]
    exact ((D w).le_opNorm v).trans (mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right (hBound w hw) (norm_nonneg v))
  have hPL (w u : E) (hw : ‖w‖ ≤ 1) (hu : ‖u‖ ≤ 1) :
      ‖DP w-DP u‖ ≤ M₂*‖w-u‖ := by
    apply ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_le_bound _ (mul_nonneg hM₂.le (norm_nonneg _))
    intro v
    change ‖T (D w v)-T (D u v)‖ ≤ (M₂*‖w-u‖)*‖v‖
    rw [← map_sub]
    change ‖J ((D w-D u) v)‖ ≤ (M₂*‖w-u‖)*‖v‖
    rw [J.norm_map]
    exact ((D w-D u).le_opNorm v).trans
      (mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right (hLip u w hu hw) (norm_nonneg v))
  let label : Lp ℝ 2 P := hlabel.toLp (fun z : E × ℝ => z.2)
  let K : S → Lp ℝ 2 P := fun w => F w.1
  let mean : Measure S → Lp ℝ 2 P := fun μ => ∫ w, K w ∂μ
  obtain ⟨hfS,hcont,havg⟩ :=
    AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Probability.GaussianPolynomialAveraging.gaussian_polynomial_parameter_average_L2 (E := E) p
  have hKint (μ : Measure S) (hμ : IsProbabilityMeasure μ) : Integrable K μ := by
    exact T.integrable_comp (havg μ hμ).2.1
  have hMeanClass (μ : Measure S) (hμ : IsProbabilityMeasure μ) :
      ∃ hpred : MemLp (fun z : E × ℝ => predictor μ z.1) 2 P,
        hpred.toLp (fun z => predictor μ z.1) = mean μ := by
    obtain ⟨hscalar,hint,hmean,hident⟩ := havg μ hμ
    let hpred : MemLp (fun z : E × ℝ => predictor μ z.1) 2 P :=
      hmean.comp_measurePreserving hmarg
    refine ⟨hpred,?_⟩
    calc
      hpred.toLp (fun z => predictor μ z.1) = T (hmean.toLp (predictor μ)) := rfl
      _ = T (∫ w, (hfS w).toLp (fun x => p.eval ⟪w.1,x⟫_ℝ) ∂μ) := congrArg T hident
      _ = mean μ := (T.integral_comp_comm hint).symm
  have hMeanAE (μ : Measure S) (hμ : IsProbabilityMeasure μ) :
      (fun z => mean μ z) =ᵐ[P] (fun z : E × ℝ => predictor μ z.1) := by
    obtain ⟨hpred,hident⟩ := hMeanClass μ hμ
    rw [← hident]
    exact hpred.coeFn_toLp
  have hResidual (μ : Measure S) (hμ : IsProbabilityMeasure μ) :
      (fun z => (mean μ-label) z) =ᵐ[P] (fun z : E × ℝ => predictor μ z.1-z.2) := by
    filter_upwards [Lp.coeFn_sub (mean μ) label,hMeanAE μ hμ,hlabel.coeFn_toLp]
      with z hs hm hy
    simp only [Pi.sub_apply] at hs
    rw [hs,hm,hy]
  have hPot (μ : Measure S) (hμ : IsProbabilityMeasure μ) :
      V μ = fun w => 2 * ⟪mean μ-label,F w⟫_ℝ := by
    funext w
    change 2 * (∫ z, (predictor μ z.1-z.2)*p.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ ∂P) = _
    rw [L2.inner_def]
    congr 1
    apply integral_congr_ae
    filter_upwards [hResidual μ hμ,(hfP w).coeFn_toLp] with z hr hw
    change F w z = p.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ at hw
    simp only [Real.inner_apply,hr,hw]
  have hTangent :=
    AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Geometry.QuadraticFeatureTangentGradient.quadratic_feature_potential_tangent_gradient
      F DP hFP M₁ M₂ hM₁.le hM₂.le hPB hPL
  have hGrad (μ : Measure S) (hμ : IsProbabilityMeasure μ) (w : E) :
      HasGradientAt (V μ) ((2 : ℝ) • (DP w).adjoint (mean μ-label)) w := by
    rw [hPot μ hμ,hasGradientAt_iff_hasFDerivAt]
    have he : InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ E ((2 : ℝ) • (DP w).adjoint (mean μ-label)) =
        (2 : ℝ) • innerSL ℝ ((DP w).adjoint (mean μ-label)) := by
      ext v
      simp [InnerProductSpace.toDual_apply_apply,innerSL_apply_apply]
    rw [he]
    exact hTangent.1 (mean μ-label) w
  refine ⟨hfP,hdfP,DP,M₁,M₂,hM₁,hM₂,hDP,hFP,hPB,hPL,?_⟩
  intro μ hμ
  refine ⟨(havg μ hμ).1,hKint μ hμ,hMeanClass μ hμ,hPot μ hμ,?_,?_⟩
  · intro w
    obtain ⟨hpred,hident⟩ := hMeanClass μ hμ
    exact ⟨(hpred.sub hlabel).integrable_mul (hfP w),hGrad μ hμ w,(hGrad μ hμ w).gradient⟩
  · intro w
    change gradient (V μ) w.1 - ⟪gradient (V μ) w.1,w.1⟫_ℝ • w.1 = _
    rw [(hGrad μ hμ w.1).gradient]
    simp only [smul_sub,real_inner_smul_left,smul_smul]
    rfl

end AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Probability.GaussianPolynomialFeatureGradient

                Samplinglib generic Gaussian feature supplement, 2026-11-17 · F7 in source-only.json; proof topology P5. (historical source) · licensed original

                Complete source statement and conditions

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel structure, and let \(\gamma_E=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\) be the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. Let \(H_j\) be the unnormalized probabilists Hermite polynomial and put \(h_j(w)=[x\mapsto H_j(\langle w,x\rangle)]\in L^2(\gamma_E)\). For a finite set \(S\subset\mathbb N\) and real coefficients \(c_j\), put \(F_{S,c}(w)=\sum_{j\in S}c_jh_j(w)\). Every finite feature map \(F_{S,c}\) is globally twice continuously Fréchet differentiable on the entire ambient space.

                • The finite-dimensional real inner-product and Borel structures are the actual structures on the same carrier \(E\).
                • \(\gamma_E\) is the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. No positive dimension restriction is imposed.
                • \(S\) is finite and \(c_j\) are arbitrary real coefficients. No unit-vector or series-convergence hypothesis is needed.

                Global C² regularity of finite Hermite features

                \[F_{S,c}\in C^2(E;L^2(\gamma_E)).\]

                Samplinglib generic Gaussian feature supplement, 2026-11-17 · F6 in source-only.json; proof topology P4. (historical source) · licensed original

                Complete source statement and conditions

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel structure, and let \(\gamma_E=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\) be the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. Let \(H_j\) be the unnormalized probabilists Hermite polynomial and put \(h_j(w)=[x\mapsto H_j(\langle w,x\rangle)]\in L^2(\gamma_E)\). For a finite set \(S\subset\mathbb N\) and real coefficients \(c_j\), put \(F_{S,c}(w)=\sum_{j\in S}c_jh_j(w)\). For every finite \(S\), arbitrary real \(c_j\), and actual unit vectors \(w,z\), the Hilbert inner product is the following diagonal sum. Signed correlations, both endpoint correlations, degree zero and empty support are included.

                • The finite-dimensional real inner-product and Borel structures are the actual structures on the same carrier \(E\).
                • \(\gamma_E\) is the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. No positive dimension restriction is imposed.
                • Both directions satisfy \(\|w\|=\|z\|=1\). They need not be independent or orthogonal.
                • \(S\) and the real coefficients are arbitrary; no parity, positivity, or total-mass normalization is imposed.

                Finite Gaussian Hermite Gram formula

                \[\langle F_{S,c}(w),F_{S,c}(z)\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_E)}=\sum_{j\in S}j!c_j^2\langle w,z\rangle^j.\]

                Read the formalized proofs

                Samplinglib mathematical lesson

                Finite Gaussian Hermite Gram formula

                Read this first

                Mathematical statement

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel structure, and let \(\gamma_E=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\) be the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. Let \(H_j\) be the unnormalized probabilists Hermite polynomial and put \(h_j(w)=[x\mapsto H_j(\langle w,x\rangle)]\in L^2(\gamma_E)\). For a finite set \(S\subset\mathbb N\) and real coefficients \(c_j\), put \(F_{S,c}(w)=\sum_{j\in S}c_jh_j(w)\).                 Complete source statement and conditions

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure, and let \(\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\). Let \(u,v\in E\) satisfy \(\|u\|=\|v\|=1\), and put \(\rho=\langle u,v\rangle\). Let \(H_k\) denote the unnormalized probabilists’ Hermite polynomial, defined by \(H_0=1\) and \(H_{k+1}(t)=tH_k(t)-H_k^{\prime}(t)\). For every pair of natural degrees \(i,j\), the literal product \(x\mapsto H_i(\langle u,x\rangle)H_j(\langle v,x\rangle)\) is absolutely integrable under \(\gamma\). Its integral is \(i!\rho^i\) if \(i=j\), and zero if \(i\ne j\). Both degrees can be zero, and coincident or antipodal unit directions are included.

                • \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel measurable structure; \(\gamma\) is its centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability.
                • \(u,v\) are actual unit vectors in the same carrier. There is no linear-independence, orthogonality or nonsingular two-dimensional density assumption.
                • \(i,j\in\mathbb N\) are arbitrary. The polynomials have integer coefficients evaluated in \(\mathbb R\) through the canonical coefficient map.
                • The correlation is the actual inner product \(\rho\in[-1,1]\). Both endpoint values and zero are allowed. Product integrability is a conclusion.

                Hermite products of correlated Gaussian projections

                \[\int_E H_i(\langle u,x\rangle)H_j(\langle v,x\rangle)\,d\gamma(x)=\begin{cases}i!\,\rho^i,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad\rho=\langle u,v\rangle.\]

                Read the formalized proofs

                Hermite products of correlated Gaussian projections

                Read this first

                Mathematical statement

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure, and let \(\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\). Let \(u,v\in E\) satisfy \(\|u\|=\|v\|=1\), and put \(\rho=\langle u,v\rangle\). Let \(H_k\) denote the unnormalized probabilists’ Hermite polynomial, defined by \(H_0=1\) and \(H_{k+1}(t)=tH_k(t)-H_k^{\prime}(t)\). For every pair of natural degrees \(i,j\), the literal product \(x\mapsto H_i(\langle u,x\rangle)H_j(\langle v,x\rangle)\) is absolutely integrable under \(\gamma\). Its integral is \(i!\rho^i\) if \(i=j\), and zero if \(i\ne j\). Both degrees can be zero, and coincident or antipodal unit directions are included.

                \[\int_E H_i(\langle u,x\rangle)H_j(\langle v,x\rangle)\,d\gamma(x)=\begin{cases}i!\,\rho^i,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad\rho=\langle u,v\rangle.\]
