                theorem gaussian_hermite_ridge_gram
    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]
    (u v : E) (hu : ‖u‖ = 1) (hv : ‖v‖ = 1) (i j : ℕ) :
    let G : E → ℝ := fun x =>
      Polynomial.aeval ⟪u,x⟫_ℝ (Polynomial.hermite i) *
        Polynomial.aeval ⟪v,x⟫_ℝ (Polynomial.hermite j)
    Integrable G (stdGaussian E) ∧
      (∫ x, G x ∂stdGaussian E) =
        if i = j then (i.factorial : ℝ) * ⟪u,v⟫_ℝ ^ i else 0

                Exact module and namespace context

                This determines mixed moments of correlated Gaussian projections. Proof strategy: Obtain integrability from polynomial Gaussian moments; Supply the full Stein domain for the product; Cancel the first derivative by the Hermite recurrence; Iterate the adjoint identity; Evaluate the equal- and lower-degree cases; Exchange the two projections when the first degree is smaller.

                Full assumptions and notation

                All objects and hypotheses

                • \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel measurable structure; \(\gamma\) is its centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability.
                • \(u,v\) are actual unit vectors in the same carrier. There is no linear-independence, orthogonality or nonsingular two-dimensional density assumption.
                • \(i,j\in\mathbb N\) are arbitrary. The polynomials have integer coefficients evaluated in \(\mathbb R\) through the canonical coefficient map.
                • The correlation is the actual inner product \(\rho\in[-1,1]\). Both endpoint values and zero are allowed. Product integrability is a conclusion.
                • When \(i=j=0\), the natural zeroth power gives integral one, even if \(\rho=0\). At \(u=v\), the equal-degree value is \(i!\); at \(u=-v\), it is \(i!(-1)^i\).
                • Dimension one is allowed. In dimension zero no unit vectors exist, so the unit-vector hypotheses are vacuous; the theorem does not create such vectors.

                Mathematical proof

                Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                1. Obtain integrability from polynomial Gaussian moments

                Every real polynomial ridge belongs to \(L^2(\gamma)\) by the existing Gaussian polynomial theorem. The product of any two such ridges is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. An extra factor \(\langle u,x\rangle\) is absorbed into the first polynomial, so the same result will supply the weighted Stein integrand.

                \[p(\langle u,\cdot\rangle),q(\langle v,\cdot\rangle)\in L^2(\gamma)\ \Longrightarrow\ p(\langle u,\cdot\rangle)q(\langle v,\cdot\rangle)\in L^1(\gamma).\]
                Corresponding Lean step
                private theorem ridge_L2 (p : Polynomial ℝ) (w : E) :
    MemLp (fun x => p.eval ⟪w,x⟫_ℝ) 2 (stdGaussian E) := by
  obtain ⟨hf, _⟩ :=
    GaussianPolynomialDifferentiation.actual_gaussian_polynomial_ridge_L2_frechet_derivative
      (E := E) p
  exact hf w

private theorem ridge_product_integrable (p q : Polynomial ℝ) (u v : E) :
    Integrable (fun x => p.eval ⟪u,x⟫_ℝ * q.eval ⟪v,x⟫_ℝ) (stdGaussian E) :=
  (ridge_L2 p u).integrable_mul (ridge_L2 q v)

                Literal excerpt from the unchanged historical public-path candidate. The complete module supplies the named local facts and remains available for whole-module review.

                2. Supply the full Stein domain for the product

                For a real polynomial \(q\), set \(f(x)=H_i(\langle u,x\rangle)q(\langle v,x\rangle)\). The chain and product rules give its derivative in direction \(u\). Unit length makes the first inner-product factor one, while the second is \(\rho\). Each derivative term is a product of polynomial ridges, so step 1 establishes all three integrability conditions of the shared Stein theorem.

                \[Df(x)[u]=H_i^{\prime}(\langle u,x\rangle)q(\langle v,x\rangle)+\rho H_i(\langle u,x\rangle)q^{\prime}(\langle v,x\rangle).\]
                Corresponding Lean step
                  have hB (x : E) : HasFDerivAt B (BD x • innerSL ℝ v) x := by
    exact (q.hasDerivAt ⟪v,x⟫_ℝ).comp_hasFDerivAt x (innerSL ℝ v).hasFDerivAt
  have hf (x : E) := (hA x).mul (hB x)
  have hf' : (fun x => fderiv ℝ f x u) = fun x => AD x * B x + ρ * (A x * BD x) := by
    funext x
    change fderiv ℝ (A * B) x u = _
    rw [(hf x).fderiv]
    simp only [ContinuousLinearMap.add_apply, ContinuousLinearMap.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul,
      innerSL_apply_apply, real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq, hu, one_pow, mul_one,
      real_inner_comm u v, ρ]
    ring
  have hx : (fun x => ⟪x,u⟫_ℝ * f x) = XB := by
    funext x
    rw [real_inner_comm u x]
    simp only [XB, f, A, eval_mul, eval_X, mul_assoc]

  have hAd : Integrable (fun x => AD x * B x) (stdGaussian E) :=
    ridge_product_integrable p.derivative q u v
  have hBd : Integrable (fun x => A x * BD x) (stdGaussian E) :=
    ridge_product_integrable p q.derivative u v

    (fun x => (hf x).differentiableAt)
    (ridge_product_integrable p q u v) (hx.symm ▸ hi)
    (hf'.symm ▸ (hAd.add (hBd.const_mul ρ)))

                3. Cancel the first derivative by the Hermite recurrence

                Apply Stein in direction \(u\). Subtract the term containing \(H_i^{\prime}\) and use \(H_{i+1}(t)=tH_i(t)-H_i^{\prime}(t)\). Only the derivative of the second polynomial remains.

                \[\int H_{i+1}(\langle u,x\rangle)q(\langle v,x\rangle)\,d\gamma=\rho\int H_i(\langle u,x\rangle)q^{\prime}(\langle v,x\rangle)\,d\gamma.\]

      filter_upwards with x
      rw [hermiteR_succ]
      simp only [p, B, AD, XB, eval_sub]
      ring
    _ = _ := by
      rw [integral_sub hi hAd]
      linarith only [hs]

                4. Iterate the adjoint identity

                Apply step 3 repeatedly, replacing \(q\) by its derivative at each step. The base case uses \(H_0=1\). After \(i\) iterations the entire Hermite factor has been moved onto an ordinary derivative of \(q\), with one factor of \(\rho\) at each iteration.

                \[\int H_i(\langle u,x\rangle)q(\langle v,x\rangle)\,d\gamma=\rho^i\int q^{(i)}(\langle v,x\rangle)\,d\gamma.\]
                Corresponding Lean step
                private theorem hermite_adjoint_iterate (u v : E) (hu : ‖u‖ = 1)

      ⟪u,v⟫_ℝ ^ i * ∫ x, (derivative^[i] q).eval ⟪v,x⟫_ℝ ∂stdGaussian E := by
  induction i generalizing q with
  | zero => simp [hermiteR, hermite_zero]
  | succ i ih =>
      rw [hermite_adjoint_step u v hu, ih q.derivative,
        Function.iterate_succ_apply, pow_succ]
      ring

                Literal excerpt from the unchanged historical public-path candidate. The complete module supplies the named local facts and remains available for whole-module review.

                5. Evaluate the equal- and lower-degree cases

                Take \(q=H_j\). If \(i=j\), monicity and degree give \(H_i^{(i)}=i!\), whose Gaussian probability integral is \(i!\). If \(i>j\), the derivative order exceeds the polynomial degree, so the integral is zero. This includes the degree-zero case.

                \[H_i^{(i)}=i!,\qquad H_j^{(i)}=0\quad(i>j).\]

      if i = j then (i.factorial : ℝ) * ⟪u,v⟫_ℝ ^ i else 0 := by

  by_cases h : i = j

    simp [mul_comm]

      (hermiteR_degree_le j).trans_lt (lt_of_le_of_ne hji (Ne.symm h))
    rw [iterate_derivative_eq_zero hn]
    simp [h]

      exact Filter.Eventually.of_forall fun _ => mul_comm _ _
    rw [hc, hermite_gram_le v u hv j i h]
    by_cases hij : i = j
    · subst j
      simp [real_inner_comm u v]
    · simp [hij, Ne.symm hij]

#print axioms gaussian_hermite_ridge_gram

end AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Probability.GaussianHermiteGram

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel structure, and let \(\gamma_E=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\) be the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. Let \(H_j\) be the unnormalized probabilists Hermite polynomial and put \(h_j(w)=[x\mapsto H_j(\langle w,x\rangle)]\in L^2(\gamma_E)\). For a finite set \(S\subset\mathbb N\) and real coefficients \(c_j\), put \(F_{S,c}(w)=\sum_{j\in S}c_jh_j(w)\).                 • The finite-dimensional real inner-product and Borel structures are the actual structures on the same carrier \(E\).
                • \(\gamma_E\) is the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. No positive dimension restriction is imposed.
                • \(j\) is arbitrary; the parameter vector is not restricted to the sphere.

                Library supplement: actual Gaussian joint-data potential gradients

                An original reusable mathematics supplement placed by subject. No primary-textbook theorem or whole-model completion claim.

                Samplinglib original Gaussian joint-data potential supplement v1,2026-10-23 · Original complete statement, conditions, definitions and seven proof steps in units[0] at immutable source commit 9ebb4f57fbdcb8db51701547ed0e0043ef743b4f. (historical source) · licensed original

                Complete source statement and conditions

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure, \(\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\) its centered standard identity-covariance Gaussian, and \(S=\{w\in E:\|w\|=1\}\). Let \(P\) be a probability law on \(E\times\mathbb R\) with first marginal \(\gamma\), and let \(p\) be a real polynomial. Assume the response \((x,y)\mapsto y\) lies in \(L^2(P)\). For each probability \(\mu\) on \(S\), define the predictor, literal scalar potential and projected ambient gradient by the displayed formulas. Write \(g_\mu=\nabla V_\mu\), and let \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) denote all probability couplings. The potential integrand is integrable and the actual ambient gradient exists at every ambient weight. There are positive constants \(C_1,C_2\), chosen before all parameter laws and unit weights, for which \(G_\mu(w)\) is tangent, \(\|G_\mu(w)\|\le C_1\), \(Q(\mu,\nu)<\infty\), and the displayed joint law/point estimate holds. The constants may depend on \(E,p,P\), including the response second moment. No independence of response and input, derivative witness, domination bound, mean bound, integral identity or gradient oracle is assumed. The cost is the explicit angular cost and the vector is the projected ambient gradient; no intrinsic path-length identity, installed manifold-gradient/Wasserstein API, generative model or full convergence theorem is asserted.

                • \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure. Completeness is derived.
                • \(P\) is a probability measure on \(E\times\mathbb R\), and its first-coordinate pushforward is exactly \(\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\).
                • \(p\) is a finite real polynomial, and \((x,y)\mapsto y\) belongs to \(L^2(P)\). No independence is required.
                • \(S=\{w:\|w\|=1\}\). The display defines the literal predictor \(f_\mu\), potential \(V_\mu\), projection \(G_\mu\), and cost \(c(w,u)=\arccos\langle w,u\rangle\).
                • \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is the set of all probability couplings. The extended nonnegative value \(Q(\mu,\nu)\) is proved finite before interpreting its real square root.

                \[\begin{gathered}\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E),\qquad S=\{w\in E:\|w\|=1\},\\f_\mu(x)=\int_S p(\langle w,x\rangle)\,d\mu(w),\\V_\mu(w)=2\int_{E\times\mathbb R}(f_\mu(x)-y)p(\langle w,x\rangle)\,dP(x,y),\\G_\mu(w)=\nabla V_\mu(w)-\langle\nabla V_\mu(w),w\rangle w,\\c(w,u)=\arccos\langle w,u\rangle,\quad Q(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{S\times S}c^2\,d\pi,\\\|G_\mu(w)\|\le C_1,\quad\|G_\mu(w)-G_\nu(u)\|\le C_2\bigl(\sqrt{Q(\mu,\nu)}+c(w,u)\bigr).\end{gathered}\]

                Samplinglib mathematical lesson

                Actual Gaussian joint-data potentials: gradients and angular transport control

                Read this first

                Mathematical statement

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure, \(\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\) its centered standard identity-covariance Gaussian, and \(S=\{w\in E:\|w\|=1\}\). Let \(P\) be a probability law on \(E\times\mathbb R\) with first marginal \(\gamma\), and let \(p\) be a real polynomial. Assume the response \((x,y)\mapsto y\) lies in \(L^2(P)\). For each probability \(\mu\) on \(S\), define the predictor, literal scalar potential and projected ambient gradient by the displayed formulas. Write \(g_\mu=\nabla V_\mu\), and let \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) denote all probability couplings. The potential integrand is integrable and the actual ambient gradient exists at every ambient weight. There are positive constants \(C_1,C_2\), chosen before all parameter laws and unit weights, for which \(G_\mu(w)\) is tangent, \(\|G_\mu(w)\|\le C_1\), \(Q(\mu,\nu)<\infty\), and the displayed joint law/point estimate holds. The constants may depend on \(E,p,P\), including the response second moment. No independence of response and input, derivative witness, domination bound, mean bound, integral identity or gradient oracle is assumed. The cost is the explicit angular cost and the vector is the projected ambient gradient; no intrinsic path-length identity, installed manifold-gradient/Wasserstein API, generative model or full convergence theorem is asserted.

                \[\begin{gathered}\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E),\qquad S=\{w\in E:\|w\|=1\},\\f_\mu(x)=\int_S p(\langle w,x\rangle)\,d\mu(w),\\V_\mu(w)=2\int_{E\times\mathbb R}(f_\mu(x)-y)p(\langle w,x\rangle)\,dP(x,y),\\G_\mu(w)=\nabla V_\mu(w)-\langle\nabla V_\mu(w),w\rangle w,\\c(w,u)=\arccos\langle w,u\rangle,\quad Q(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{S\times S}c^2\,d\pi,\\\|G_\mu(w)\|\le C_1,\quad\|G_\mu(w)-G_\nu(u)\|\le C_2\bigl(\sqrt{Q(\mu,\nu)}+c(w,u)\bigr).\end{gathered}\]
                Lean statement · gaussian_polynomial_joint_potential_projected_gradient_transport_control

                Let E be a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel structure, let γ=stdGaussian(E) be its centered standard identity-covariance Gaussian, and let S={w in E: norm(w)=1}. Let P be a probability law on E×ℝ with first marginal γ, p a finite real polynomial, and the actual response (x,y)↦y square-integrable under P. For each parameter probability μ on S, define f_μ(x)=∫_S p(inner(w,x))dμ(w), V_μ(w)=2∫(f_μ(x)−y)p(inner(w,x))dP(x,y), g_μ(w)=gradient(V_μ)(w), and G_μ(w)=g_μ(w)−inner(g_μ(w),w)w. For w,u in S define c(w,u)=arccos(inner(w,u)); let Π(μ,ν) be all probability measures on S×S with marginals μ,ν, and Q(μ,ν)=inf_{π in Π(μ,ν)}∫c²dπ, an extended nonnegative cost. Then the integrand defining V_μ is integrable at every ambient weight and its actual ambient gradient exists there. There are positive C₁,C₂, chosen before all parameter laws and unit weights, such that G_μ(w) is tangent, norm(G_μ(w))≤C₁, Q(μ,ν) is finite, and norm(G_μ(w)−G_ν(u))≤C₂(sqrt(Q(μ,ν))+c(w,u)). No independence of response/input or derivative, domination, mean-bound, integral-identity or gradient oracle is assumed. Constants may depend on E,p,P, including the response L² norm. The theorem concerns the explicit angular cost and projected ambient gradient; it does not assert an intrinsic path-length identity, an installed manifold-gradient/Wasserstein API, teacher/noise construction or full model convergence.

    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]
    (P : Measure (E × ℝ)) [IsProbabilityMeasure P]
    (hGaussian : P.map Prod.fst = ProbabilityTheory.stdGaussian E)
    (p : Polynomial ℝ) (hlabel : MemLp (fun z : E × ℝ => z.2) 2 P) :
    let S := {w : E // ‖w‖ = 1}
    let predictor : Measure S → E → ℝ := fun μ x => ∫ w, p.eval ⟪w.1,x⟫_ℝ ∂μ
    let V : Measure S → E → ℝ := fun μ w =>
      2 * ∫ z, (predictor μ z.1-z.2)*p.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ ∂P
    let grad : Measure S → E → E := fun μ w => gradient (V μ) w
    let G : Measure S → E → E := fun μ w => grad μ w-⟪grad μ w,w⟫_ℝ • w
    let c : S × S → ℝ := fun z => Real.arccos ⟪z.1.1,z.2.1⟫_ℝ
    let Q : Measure S → Measure S → ℝ≥0∞ := fun μ ν =>
      AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.Transport.transportCost
        (fun z => ENNReal.ofReal ((c z)^2)) μ ν
    ∃ C₁ C₂ : ℝ, 0 < C₁ ∧ 0 < C₂ ∧
      (∀ μ : Measure S, IsProbabilityMeasure μ →
        (∀ w : E, Integrable (fun z : E × ℝ =>
            (predictor μ z.1-z.2)*p.eval ⟪w,z.1⟫_ℝ) P ∧
          HasGradientAt (V μ) (grad μ w) w) ∧
        ∀ w : S, ⟪w.1,G μ w.1⟫_ℝ = 0 ∧ ‖G μ w.1‖ ≤ C₁) ∧
      ∀ μ ν : Measure S, IsProbabilityMeasure μ → IsProbabilityMeasure ν →
        Q μ ν ≠ ∞ ∧ ∀ w u : S,
          ‖G μ w.1-G ν u.1‖ ≤
            C₂*((Q μ ν ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ)).toReal+c (w,u))

                Complete source statement and conditions

                Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel structure, and let \(\gamma_E=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\) be the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. For every real polynomial \(p\) and every \(w\in E\), the literal function \(x\mapsto p(\langle w,x\rangle)\) belongs to \(L^2(\gamma_E)\). Its equivalence-class map is globally \(C^\infty\) on all of \(E\). The membership witnesses are produced by the proof and used to form these actual classes.

                • The finite-dimensional real inner-product and Borel structures are the actual structures on the same carrier \(E\).
                • \(\gamma_E\) is the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. No positive dimension restriction is imposed.
                • \(p\) has arbitrary real coefficients and arbitrary finite degree; \(w\) is any ambient vector.

                Smooth polynomial features in Gaussian L²

                \[E\longrightarrow L^2(\gamma_E),\qquad w\longmapsto[x\mapsto p(\langle w,x\rangle)]\quad\text{is }C^\infty.\]

                Exact module and namespace context

                This supplies the regularity or moment identity needed to use actual Gaussian feature classes. Proof strategy: Build smooth powers in every finite integrability exponent; Assemble the polynomial; Identify the literal L² class.

                Full assumptions and notation

                All objects and hypotheses

                • The finite-dimensional real inner-product and Borel structures are the actual structures on the same carrier \(E\).
                • \(\gamma_E\) is the centered identity-covariance Gaussian probability. No positive dimension restriction is imposed.
                • \(p\) has arbitrary real coefficients and arbitrary finite degree; \(w\) is any ambient vector.

                Mathematical proof

                Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                1. Build smooth powers in every finite integrability exponent

                Prove the power claim simultaneously for every finite \(q\ge1\). Constants give degree zero. Gaussian projection moments supply a linear map into \(L^{2q}\); finite-dimensionality makes it continuous and smooth. Multiply the lower power and the projection by the continuous Hölder bilinear map.

                \[L^{2q}(\gamma_E)\times L^{2q}(\gamma_E)\longrightarrow L^q(\gamma_E),\qquad(f,g)\longmapsto fg.\]
                Corresponding Lean step
                private theorem smooth_power_ridge (n : ℕ) (q : ℝ≥0∞) [Fact (1 ≤ q)] (hqtop : q ≠ ⊤) :
    ∃ F : E → Lp ℝ q (stdGaussian E), ContDiff ℝ (∞ : ℕ∞ω) F ∧
      ∀ w, (F w : E → ℝ) =ᵐ[stdGaussian E] fun x => ⟪w, x⟫_ℝ ^ n := by
  let μ := stdGaussian E
  induction n generalizing q with
  | zero =>
    have h : MemLp (fun _ : E => (1 : ℝ)) q μ := memLp_const _
    exact ⟨fun _ => h.toLp _, contDiff_const, fun w => by
      simpa only [pow_zero] using h.coeFn_toLp⟩
  | succ n ih =>
    have hq' : 1 ≤ 2 * q := (Fact.out : 1 ≤ q).trans (by rw [two_mul]; exact le_add_of_nonneg_right bot_le)
    have hq'top : 2 * q ≠ ⊤ := ENNReal.mul_ne_top (by norm_num) hqtop
    have : Fact (1 ≤ 2 * q) := ⟨hq'⟩
    have : ENNReal.HolderTriple (2 * q) (2 * q) q := ⟨by
      rw [ENNReal.mul_inv (.inl (by norm_num : (2 : ℝ≥0∞) ≠ 0))
        (.inl (by norm_num : (2 : ℝ≥0∞) ≠ ⊤)), ← add_mul, ← two_mul,
        ENNReal.mul_inv_cancel (by norm_num : (2 : ℝ≥0∞) ≠ 0) (by norm_num), one_mul]⟩
    obtain ⟨F, hF, hFa⟩ := ih (2 * q) hq'top
    have hlin (w : E) : MemLp (fun x : E => ⟪w, x⟫_ℝ) (2 * q) μ :=
      IsGaussian.memLp_dual μ (innerSL ℝ w) (2 * q) hq'top
    let L : E →ₗ[ℝ] Lp ℝ (2 * q) μ :=
      { toFun := fun w => (hlin w).toLp _
        map_add' := by
          intro u v
          apply Lp.ext
          filter_upwards [(hlin (u + v)).coeFn_toLp, (hlin u).coeFn_toLp,
            (hlin v).coeFn_toLp, Lp.coeFn_add ((hlin u).toLp _) ((hlin v).toLp _)]
            with x huv hu hv hsum
          rw [huv, hsum, Pi.add_apply, hu, hv, inner_add_left]
        map_smul' := by
          intro c w
          apply Lp.ext
          filter_upwards [(hlin (c • w)).coeFn_toLp, (hlin w).coeFn_toLp,
            Lp.coeFn_smul c ((hlin w).toLp _)] with x hcw hw hsmul
          rw [RingHom.id_apply, hcw, hsmul, Pi.smul_apply, hw, real_inner_smul_left, smul_eq_mul] }
    let B := ContinuousLinearMap.mul ℝ ℝ
    let M := B.holderL μ (2 * q) (2 * q) q
    refine ⟨fun w => M (F w) (L w), ?_, ?_⟩
    · exact (M.contDiff.comp hF).clm_apply L.toContinuousLinearMap.contDiff
    · intro w
      change ⇑(B.holder q (F w) ((hlin w).toLp _)) =ᵐ[μ] _
      filter_upwards [B.coeFn_holder (r := q) (F w) ((hlin w).toLp _), hFa w, (hlin w).coeFn_toLp]
        with x hmul hf hl
      rw [hmul, hf, hl, pow_succ]

                Exact contiguous excerpt. The complete module supplies the surrounding parameters and local facts.

                2. Assemble the polynomial

                Polynomial induction builds the map using sums and scalar multiples of the smooth power maps. The almost-everywhere representative formulas are preserved at each step.

                \[[p(\langle w,\cdot\rangle)]=\sum_{j\in\operatorname{supp}p}p_j[\langle w,\cdot\rangle^j].\]
                Corresponding Lean step
                    induction p using Polynomial.induction_on' with
    | add p r hp hr =>
      obtain ⟨F, hF, hFa⟩ := hp
      obtain ⟨G, hG, hGa⟩ := hr
      refine ⟨fun w => F w + G w, hF.add hG, fun w => ?_⟩
      filter_upwards [Lp.coeFn_add (F w) (G w), hFa w, hGa w] with x hsum hf hg
      simp only [hsum, Pi.add_apply, hf, hg, Polynomial.eval_add]
    | monomial n c =>
      obtain ⟨F, hF, hFa⟩ := smooth_power_ridge (E := E) n 2 (by norm_num)
      refine ⟨fun w => c • F w, hF.const_smul c, fun w => ?_⟩
      filter_upwards [Lp.coeFn_smul c (F w), hFa w] with x hsmul hf
      simp only [hsmul, Pi.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul, hf, Polynomial.eval_monomial]
  obtain ⟨F, hF, hFa⟩ := representation
  let h : ∀ w : E, MemLp (fun x : E => p.eval ⟪w, x⟫_ℝ) 2 (stdGaussian E) :=
    fun w => (memLp_congr_ae (hFa w)).1 (Lp.memLp (F w))

                Exact contiguous excerpt. The complete module supplies the surrounding parameters and local facts.

                3. Identify the literal L² class

                The constructed map has the literal polynomial ridge as an almost-everywhere representative. Transfer square integrability along that equality and use extensionality of the quotient to identify the produced map with the stated class map.

                \[F(w)=[x\mapsto p(\langle w,x\rangle)]\quad\text{in }L^2(\gamma_E).\]
                Corresponding Lean step
                  refine ⟨h, ?_⟩
  convert hF using 1
  funext w
  exact Lp.ext ((h w).coeFn_toLp.trans (hFa w).symm)

                  Smooth Gaussian polynomial data potentials

                  Original Samplinglib derivation from existing Gaussian L2 smoothness, actual potential representation and compact derivative bounds. The linked parent is not presented as an external proof of the new all-order estimate.

                  Samplinglib original statistical-model supplement, 2026-11-18; Lean 4.33.0 · Original statement in runs/20261118-gaussian-potential-smooth/source-statement.txt. The pinned linked parent proves the actual joint-feature representation. (historical source) · licensed original

                  Complete source statement and conditions

                  Let E be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let (X,Y) have joint probability law P, with X standard Gaussian and Y square integrable. For any real polynomial p and any probability rho on the unit sphere S, define the predictor and actual data potential by the integrals below. The potential V_rho is smooth on all of E. For every real radius R and derivative order n, there is a finite nonnegative constant C, chosen before rho and w, that bounds the norm of D^n V_rho(w) for every sphere probability rho and every ambient w with norm at most R.

                  • E is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel sigma algebra. No positive dimension is assumed; an empty sphere has no probability law to instantiate.
                  • P is a probability on E times R whose first marginal is exactly the standard Gaussian on E. The label Y is in L2(P); no independence or higher label moment is assumed.
                  • p is any real polynomial. No parity, coefficient normalization, prescribed degree cutoff or conditional teacher relation is assumed.
                  • For each R and n, the bound C may depend on P, p, E, R and n, but is uniform over rho and w. Order zero is included; a negative radius gives an empty spatial condition.

                  Smoothness and common local derivative bounds

                  \[\begin{gathered}V_\rho\in C^\infty(E;\mathbb R)\quad(\rho\in\mathcal P(S)),\\\forall R\in\mathbb R\ \forall n\in\mathbb N\ \exists C\ge0:\\\forall\rho\in\mathcal P(S)\ \forall w\in E,\\\|w\|\le R\ \Longrightarrow\ \|D^nV_\rho(w)\|\le C.\end{gathered}\]

    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]
    (P : Measure (E × ℝ)) [IsProbabilityMeasure P]
    (hGaussian : P.map Prod.fst = stdGaussian E)
    (p : Polynomial ℝ) (hlabel : MemLp (fun z : E × ℝ => z.2) 2 P) :
    let S := {w : E // ‖w‖ = 1}
    let V : Measure S → E → ℝ := fun ρ w =>
      2 * ∫ z : E × ℝ,
        ((∫ v : S, p.eval ⟪(v : E), z.1⟫_ℝ ∂ρ) - z.2) *
          p.eval ⟪w, z.1⟫_ℝ ∂P
    (∀ ρ : Measure S, IsProbabilityMeasure ρ → ContDiff ℝ (∞ : ℕ∞ω) (V ρ)) ∧
    ∀ (R : ℝ) (n : ℕ), ∃ C : ℝ, 0 ≤ C ∧
      ∀ ρ : Measure S, IsProbabilityMeasure ρ →
        ∀ w : E, ‖w‖ ≤ R → ‖iteratedFDeriv ℝ n (V ρ) w‖ ≤ C

                  Exact module and namespace context

                  A changing parameter distribution should not require a new spatial bound at every time. The proof keeps one smooth Gaussian feature map and controls every law-dependent residual by the same norm estimate.

                  Full assumptions and notation

                  All objects and hypotheses

                  • E is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel sigma algebra. No positive dimension is assumed; an empty sphere has no probability law to instantiate.
                  • P is a probability on E times R whose first marginal is exactly the standard Gaussian on E. The label Y is in L2(P); no independence or higher label moment is assumed.
                  • p is any real polynomial. No parity, coefficient normalization, prescribed degree cutoff or conditional teacher relation is assumed.
                  • For each R and n, the bound C may depend on P, p, E, R and n, but is uniform over rho and w. Order zero is included; a negative radius gives an empty spatial condition.

                  Notation and interpretation

                  S and f_rho

                  S is the unit sphere; f_rho is the sphere-averaged polynomial predictor.

                  \[S=\{v\in E:\|v\|=1\},\qquad f_\rho(x)=\int_S p(\langle v,x\rangle)\,d\rho(v).\]
                  V_rho

                  The actual joint-data integral potential, evaluated at any ambient point w.

                  \[V_\rho(w)=2\int_{E\times\mathbb R}(f_\rho(x)-y)p(\langle w,x\rangle)\,dP(x,y).\]
                  D^n and its norm

                  The iterated Frechet derivative and its multilinear operator norm. Smoothness is proved, so the total Lean operators are classical derivatives here. At order zero the norm is the absolute value of the potential.

                  \[\|D^0V_\rho(w)\|=|V_\rho(w)|.\]
                  H, F, ell and m_rho

                  H is joint-data L2; F is the polynomial feature class, ell is the label class, and m_rho is the Bochner mean of the feature.

                  \[\begin{gathered}H=L^2(P),\quad F(w)=[(x,y)\mapsto p(\langle w,x\rangle)],\\\ell=[Y],\qquad m_\rho=\int_S F(v)\,d\rho(v).\end{gathered}\]

                  Mathematical proof

                  Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                  1. Pull the smooth Gaussian feature into joint-data L2

                  The existing polynomial ridge theorem gives a smooth map into Gaussian L2. Pullback by the first coordinate is a linear isometry into H, because the input marginal is exactly Gaussian. Its image is the actual polynomial feature class F. The membership witnesses are proof-irrelevant; no response differentiation or extra response moment is used.

                  \[F:E\longrightarrow L^2(P)\text{ is }C^\infty.\]

                  3. Bound every residual uniformly over the parameter law

                  Continuity of F on the compact unit ball gives a nonnegative bound B. Integrating its norm against a probability law bounds every feature mean by B. The label has one fixed finite L2 norm, so every residual and every pairing functional have the same bound.

                  \[\begin{aligned}\|m_\rho\|_H&\le B,\\\|m_\rho-\ell\|_H&\le B+\|\ell\|_H,\\\|L_\rho\|&\le2(B+\|\ell\|_H).\end{aligned}\]

  let label : Lp ℝ 2 P := hlabel.toLp (fun z : E × ℝ => z.2)

    ⟨measurable_fst, hGaussian⟩
  let J : Lp ℝ 2 (stdGaussian E) →ₗᵢ[ℝ] Lp ℝ 2 P :=
    Lp.compMeasurePreservingₗᵢ ℝ Prod.fst hmarg

    have he : F = fun w => J ((hg w).toLp (fun x : E => p.eval ⟪w, x⟫_ℝ)) := by

    rw [he]

    rw [hV ρ hρ]
    rfl

  · rw [hVL ρ hρ]
    exact (L ρ).contDiff.comp hF
  · obtain ⟨B, hB⟩ := (isCompact_closedBall (0 : E) 1).exists_bound_of_continuousOn
      hF.continuous.continuousOn
    have hB0 : 0 ≤ B := (norm_nonneg (F 0)).trans (hB 0 (by simp))

                  Library supplement: Gaussian integration by parts on its integrable domain

                  Original generic exposition of a classical Gaussian identity; existing local proof reused without a novelty or primary-textbook completion claim.

                  Samplinglib generic Gaussian analysis supplement, 2026-11-17 · Complete source-only-stein.json statement and proof topology. (historical source) · licensed original

                  Complete source statement and conditions

                  Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure, and let \(\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\). Fix a function \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) that is Fréchet differentiable everywhere and any direction \(v\in E\). Assume that each of \(f\), \(x\mapsto\langle x,v\rangle f(x)\), and \(x\mapsto Df(x)[v]\) is absolutely integrable under \(\gamma\). Then the weighted value and the directional derivative have the same Gaussian integral. No positive-dimension or unit-direction restriction is imposed.

                  • \(E\) is a real inner-product normed space of finite dimension, with its Borel measurable structure. Its completeness is derived.
                  • \(\gamma\) is the actual centered Gaussian probability with identity covariance on \(E\).
                  • \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) is Fréchet differentiable at every point, and \(v\in E\) is arbitrary, including zero.
                  • \(\int_E|f|\,d\gamma<\infty\), \(\int_E|\langle x,v\rangle f(x)|\,d\gamma<\infty\), and \(\int_E|Df(x)[v]|\,d\gamma<\infty\). All three belong to this theorem’s stated domain.

                  Gaussian integration by parts on its integrable domain

                  \[\int_E\langle x,v\rangle f(x)\,d\gamma(x)=\int_E Df(x)[v]\,d\gamma(x).\]

                  Exact module and namespace context

                  This supplies the integration identity used in the Hermite product calculation. Proof strategy: Identify and differentiate the actual Gaussian density; Transfer the stated integrability domain to Lebesgue measure; Move the derivative and cancel the sign.

                  Full assumptions and notation

                  All objects and hypotheses

                  • \(E\) is a real inner-product normed space of finite dimension, with its Borel measurable structure. Its completeness is derived.
                  • \(\gamma\) is the actual centered Gaussian probability with identity covariance on \(E\).
                  • \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) is Fréchet differentiable at every point, and \(v\in E\) is arbitrary, including zero.
                  • \(\int_E|f|\,d\gamma<\infty\), \(\int_E|\langle x,v\rangle f(x)|\,d\gamma<\infty\), and \(\int_E|Df(x)[v]|\,d\gamma<\infty\). All three belong to this theorem’s stated domain.

                  Mathematical proof

                  Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                  1. Identify and differentiate the actual Gaussian density

                  Write \(d=\dim_{\mathbb R}E\). The existing Gaussian density theorem identifies \(\gamma\) with \(\omega\,dx\). Differentiating the exponential of the squared norm gives the directional derivative shown below; the normalizing constant is independent of the evaluation point.

                  \[\omega(x)=\bigl(\sqrt{2\pi}^{\,-1}\bigr)^d e^{-\|x\|^2/2},\qquad \gamma=\omega\,dx,\qquad D\omega(x)[v]=-\omega(x)\langle x,v\rangle.\]
                  Corresponding Lean step
                  private def standardWeight (x : E) : ℝ :=
  ((Real.sqrt (2 * Real.pi))⁻¹) ^ Module.finrank ℝ E * Real.exp (-‖x‖^2 / 2)

private theorem standardWeight_pos (x : E) : 0 < standardWeight x := by
  dsimp [standardWeight]
  positivity

private theorem standardGaussian_density :
    stdGaussian E = (volume : Measure E).withDensity
      (fun x => ENNReal.ofReal (standardWeight x)) := by
  have h := AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.IsotropicGaussianDensity.map_sqrt_smul_stdGaussian_eq_withDensity
    (E := E) 1 (by norm_num)
  simpa only [Real.sqrt_one, one_smul, Measure.map_id', mul_one,
    standardWeight] using h

                  Literal density definition and identification. The density derivative is proved in the same module at lines 50–67 and is used in the next excerpt.

                  2. Transfer the stated integrability domain to Lebesgue measure

                  Because \(\omega\) is positive, Gaussian integrability of a scalar function gives Lebesgue integrability after multiplication by \(\omega\). Apply this to the three assumed functions. The density derivative identifies the third weighted product, with its minus sign.

                  \[\omega f,\quad\omega Df[ v ],\quad D\omega[v]f=-\omega\langle x,v\rangle f\quad\text{are Lebesgue integrable}.\]
                  Corresponding Lean step
                    let : CompleteSpace E := FiniteDimensional.complete ℝ E
  have hDw (x : E) : fderiv ℝ (standardWeight : E → ℝ) x v =
      -standardWeight x*inner ℝ x v := by
    rw [(standardWeight_hasFDerivAt x).fderiv]
    simp only [smul_apply, smul_eq_mul, innerSL_apply_apply]
  have hwp := standardGaussian_weighted_integrable hfi
  have hwdf := standardGaussian_weighted_integrable hdf
  have hwxf := standardGaussian_weighted_integrable hxf
  have hDwf : Integrable (fun x => fderiv ℝ (standardWeight : E → ℝ) x v*f x)
      (volume : Measure E) := by
    convert hwxf.neg using 1
    ext x
    rw [hDw]
    simp only [Pi.neg_apply]
    ring

                  Literal excerpt from the unchanged historical public-path candidate. The complete module supplies the named local facts and remains available for whole-module review.

                  3. Move the derivative and cancel the sign

                  The two differentiable functions \(\omega\) and \(f\) satisfy the full-space integration-by-parts domain. Transfer the derivative from \(f\) to \(\omega\), substitute the derivative from step 1, and convert both weighted Lebesgue integrals back to Gaussian integrals.

                  \[\int_E\omega Df[v]\,dx=-\int_E D\omega[v]f\,dx=\int_E\omega\langle x,v\rangle f\,dx.\]
                  Corresponding Lean step
                    have hparts := integral_mul_fderiv_eq_neg_fderiv_mul_of_integrable hDwf hwdf hwp
    (fun x _ => (standardWeight_hasFDerivAt x).differentiableAt)
    (fun x _ => hf x)
  rw [standardGaussian_weighted_integral, standardGaussian_weighted_integral]
  calc
    (∫ x, standardWeight x*(inner ℝ x v*f x)) =
        -(∫ x, fderiv ℝ (standardWeight : E → ℝ) x v*f x) := by
      rw [← integral_neg]
      apply integral_congr_ae
      filter_upwards with x
      rw [hDw]
      ring
    _ = ∫ x, standardWeight x*fderiv ℝ f x v := hparts.symm

                  An Introduction to Optimization on Smooth Manifolds, 2023 · sphere geometry, geodesics, and the Riemannian exponential map · faithful paraphrase

                  Complete source statement (Samplinglib restatement)

                  In a real inner-product space, the standard trigonometric curve gives the signed unit-sphere geodesic. It is smooth, agrees with the ambient exponential formula at nonnegative time, preserves unit norm for tangent increments, and has explicit derivatives and uniform bounds through order four.

                  • The ambient space is a real normed additive commutative group with an inner product.
                  • Norm preservation assumes a unit base point and an orthogonal tangent increment.
                  • The displayed closed derivative bundle assumes nonzero velocity; zero velocity is the constant curve.

                  \[\operatorname{Exp}_w(z)=\cos(\|z\|)w+\operatorname{sinc}(\|z\|)z\]

                  derivative envelope

                  \[\|\gamma^{(q)}(t)\|\le2\|z\|^q,\qquad q=1,2,3,4\]

                          Full assumptions and notation

                          All objects and hypotheses

                          • t is nonnegative.
                          • Zero time and zero velocity are allowed.
                          • w and z are arbitrary ambient vectors.

                          Mathematical proof

                          1. Handle degenerate cases

                          When t=0 or z=0, both sides reduce to w.

                          \[t=0\text{ or }z=0\Rightarrow\operatorname{Exp}_w(tz)=w\]
                          Corresponding Lean step

                          Lean discharges both branches by simplification.

                          2. Rewrite the scaled norm

                          Nonnegative t gives ‖tz‖=t‖z‖.

                          \[\|tz\|=t\|z\|\]
                          Corresponding Lean step

                          norm_smul and abs_of_nonneg prove the equality.

                          3. Expand sinc and cancel t

                          For nonzero t‖z‖, sinc becomes sine divided by its argument.

                          \[\operatorname{sinc}(t\|z\|)(tz)=\frac{\sin(t\|z\|)}{\|z\|}z\]
                          Corresponding Lean step

                          Real.sinc_of_ne_zero and field simplification finish.

                          theorem unitSphereExp_smul_eq_unitSphereGeodesic
    (w z : E) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    unitSphereExp w (t • z) = unitSphereGeodesic w z t := by
  by_cases hz : z = 0
  · subst z
    simp [unitSphereExp, unitSphereGeodesic]
  by_cases ht0 : t = 0
  · subst t
    simp [unitSphereExp, unitSphereGeodesic]
  have hr : ‖z‖ ≠ 0 := norm_ne_zero_iff.mpr hz
  have htne : t ≠ 0 := ht0
  have hnorm : ‖t • z‖ = t * ‖z‖ := by
    rw [norm_smul, Real.norm_eq_abs, abs_of_nonneg ht]
  rw [unitSphereExp, unitSphereGeodesic, if_neg hr, hnorm,
    Real.sinc_of_ne_zero (mul_ne_zero htne hr)]
  congr 1
  rw [smul_smul]
  congr 1
  field_simp [htne, hr]

      simp [real_inner_smul_left, real_inner_smul_right, htan]
    have hpyth :
        ‖unitSphereExp w z‖ ^ (2 : ℕ) =
          ‖Real.cos ‖z‖ • w‖ ^ (2 : ℕ) +
          ‖Real.sinc ‖z‖ • z‖ ^ (2 : ℕ) := by
      rw [unitSphereExp, norm_add_sq_real, hcross]
      ring
    have hfirst :
        ‖Real.cos ‖z‖ • w‖ ^ (2 : ℕ) =
          Real.cos ‖z‖ ^ (2 : ℕ) := by
      simp [norm_smul, hw, sq_abs]
    have hsinc :
        Real.sinc ‖z‖ = Real.sin ‖z‖ / ‖z‖ :=
      Real.sinc_of_ne_zero hr
    have hsecond :
        ‖Real.sinc ‖z‖ • z‖ ^ (2 : ℕ) =
          Real.sin ‖z‖ ^ (2 : ℕ) := by
      rw [norm_smul, Real.norm_eq_abs, hsinc]
      have hrpos : 0 < ‖z‖ := norm_pos_iff.mpr hz
      rw [abs_div, abs_of_pos hrpos]
      rw [div_mul_cancel₀ _ hr]
      exact sq_abs (Real.sin ‖z‖)
    have hsq : ‖unitSphereExp w z‖ ^ (2 : ℕ) = 1 := by
      rw [hpyth, hfirst, hsecond]
      nlinarith [Real.sin_sq_add_cos_sq ‖z‖]
    have hnonneg : 0 ≤ ‖unitSphereExp w z‖ := norm_nonneg _
    nlinarith


end

                                Second-order necessary conditions on the unit sphere

                                The standard second-order necessary condition and sphere restriction are textbook calculus/Riemannian optimization; Samplinglib supplies the Lean bridge to Mathlib total derivatives and explicit trace hypotheses.

                                An Introduction to Optimization on Smooth Manifolds, 2023; Mathlib v4.33.0 · second-order necessary optimality conditions and unit-sphere exponential curves · faithful paraphrase

                                Complete source statement (Samplinglib restatement)

                                A continuous real function has nonnegative double derivative at a local minimum and nonpositive double derivative at a local maximum. On the unit sphere, restricting a global extremum to tangent exponential curves yields the corresponding sign for every supplied Hessian diagonal, hence for its finite trace.

                                • Scalar extrema use continuity at the extremum and Mathlib’s total deriv (deriv f).
                                • Sphere extrema use a unit base point, tangent directions, continuity along each exponential curve, exact diagonal identities, and a finite trace identity.
                                • No PDE or model-specific coefficient occurs.

                                scalar necessary condition

                                \[x\text{ local min}\Rightarrow f^{\prime\prime}(x)\ge0,\qquad x\text{ local max}\Rightarrow f^{\prime\prime}(x)\le0\]

                                sphere trace sign

                                \[\Delta f(w)=\sum_i (f\circ\operatorname{Exp}_w(tz_i))^{\prime\prime}(0)\gtreqless0\]

                                Read the formalized proofs

                                Each statement and proof below has its own closed Lean disclosure. Samplinglib parents, Mathlib calls and external mathematical sources are distinguished in each proof.

                                Second derivative at a local minimum

                                AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Geometry.SphereSecondOrder.IsLocalMin.deriv_deriv_nonneg_of_continuousAt · theorem · Teaching coverage

                                Read this first

                                Mathematical statement

                                For a real function continuous at a local minimum, the second derivative represented by deriv (deriv f) is nonnegative.

                                \[x\text{ local min of }f,\ f\text{ continuous at }x\Longrightarrow (\operatorname{deriv}\operatorname{deriv}f)(x)\ge0\]
                                Lean statement · deriv_deriv_nonneg_of_continuousAt

                                The Lean theorem states the displayed necessary sign with every continuity, tangency, diagonal, and trace premise explicit.

                                Braces mark parameters Lean can infer; square brackets request structures such as a measurable space or probability measure. Named hypotheses are mathematical premises, not facts established by this declaration. Section parameters are described in the mathematical hypotheses above; the module link retains their exact source context.

                                Download module (.lean)
                                theorem IsLocalMin.deriv_deriv_nonneg_of_continuousAt
    {f : ℝ → ℝ} {x : ℝ} (hmin : IsLocalMin f x)
    (hc : ContinuousAt f x) :
    0 ≤ deriv (deriv f) x

                                Exact module and namespace context

                                Proof roadmap
                                1. 1Rule out a negative second derivative
                                2. 2Combine the two local inequalities
                                3. 3Differentiate the local equality twice
                                Full assumptions and notation

                                All objects and hypotheses

                                • f is a real-valued function on the real line.
                                • x is a local minimum of f.
                                • f is continuous at x; Mathlib deriv is total and equals zero at nondifferentiable points.

                                Mathematical proof

                                1. Rule out a negative second derivative

                                If the second derivative were negative, Mathlib’s strict second-derivative test would also make x a local maximum.

                                \[f^{\prime\prime}(x)<0\Longrightarrow x\text{ is a local maximum}\]
                                Corresponding Lean step

                                Use isLocalMax_of_deriv_deriv_neg, with Fermat’s identity at the local minimum.

                                2. Combine the two local inequalities

                                A point that is both a local minimum and a local maximum has a neighborhood on which f is constant.

                                \[f(x)\le f(y)\le f(x)\Longrightarrow f(y)=f(x)\]
                                Corresponding Lean step

                                Intersect the two neighborhood filters and apply antisymmetry.

                                3. Differentiate the local equality twice

                                The derivative is locally zero, hence its derivative at x is zero, contradicting strict negativity.

                                \[f\equiv f(x)\text{ locally}\Longrightarrow f^\prime\equiv0\text{ locally}\Longrightarrow f^{\prime\prime}(x)=0\]
                                Corresponding Lean step

                                Filter.EventuallyEq.deriv and deriv_eq transport the local equality.

                                Lean verification

                                The exact proof begins folded immediately after the mathematical argument; the statement is folded beside the claim above.

                                Lean proof · deriv_deriv_nonneg_of_continuousAt

                                The proof reduces a forbidden strict sign to simultaneous local minimum and maximum, or restricts the sphere extremum to feasible exponential curves and sums the scalar signs.

                                Braces mark parameters Lean can infer; square brackets request structures such as a measurable space or probability measure. Named hypotheses are mathematical premises, not facts established by this declaration. Section parameters are described in the mathematical hypotheses above; the module link retains their exact source context.

                                Download module (.lean)
                                theorem IsLocalMin.deriv_deriv_nonneg_of_continuousAt
    {f : ℝ → ℝ} {x : ℝ} (hmin : IsLocalMin f x)
    (hc : ContinuousAt f x) :
    0 ≤ deriv (deriv f) x := by
  by_contra hnonneg
  have hneg : deriv (deriv f) x < 0 := lt_of_not_ge hnonneg
  have hmax : IsLocalMax f x :=
    isLocalMax_of_deriv_deriv_neg hneg hmin.deriv_eq_zero hc
  have hconst : f =ᶠ[𝓝 x] fun _ : ℝ => f x := by
    filter_upwards [hmin, hmax] with y hymin hymax
    exact le_antisymm hymax hymin
  have hderiv : deriv f =ᶠ[𝓝 x] fun _ : ℝ => 0 := by
    simpa using hconst.deriv
  have hzero : deriv (deriv f) x = 0 := by
    calc
      deriv (deriv f) x = deriv (fun _ : ℝ => 0) x := hderiv.deriv_eq
      _ = 0 := by simp
  linarith

                                    Full assumptions and notation

                                    All objects and hypotheses

                                    • w has unit norm and every direction z_i is tangent at w.
                                    • f has a global minimum on the unit sphere at w.

                                    Mathematical proof

                                    1. Keep every curve on the sphere

                                    Unit norm and tangency make Exp_w(t z_i) a sphere point for every real t.

                                    \[\|\operatorname{Exp}_w(tz_i)\|=1\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step

                                    Apply unitSphereExp_norm_eq_one after scaling the tangent direction.

                                    2. Restrict the minimum to each curve

                                    The global sphere minimum becomes a local minimum of every scalar curve at t=0.

                                    \[f(w)\le f(\operatorname{Exp}_w(tz_i))\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step

                                    Build an IsLocalMin from the global IsMinOn inequality.

                                    3. Sum the directional signs

                                    The real second-order necessary condition makes every diagonal entry nonnegative; a finite sum preserves the sign.

                                    \[0\le h_i\ \forall i\Longrightarrow0\le\sum_i h_i=\Delta f(w)\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step

                                    Rewrite each diagonal identity and use Finset.sum_nonneg.

                                    Reflection symmetry of the spherical differential expression

                                    Original Samplinglib derivation from the pinned operator definition and Mathlib derivative transport. The linked file defines the operator; it is not presented as an external proof of this new bundled statement.

                                    Samplinglib original shared mathematical supplement, 2026-11-18; Lean 4.33.0 · Original reflection identity stated in runs/20261118-sphere-antipodal-generator/source-statement.txt.                                     Complete source statement and conditions

                                    Let A(x)=-x on E=R^I, where I is finite. For every real-valued ambient function f and every w,h∈E, the first derivative of f∘A at w applied to h equals -Df(-w)[h]. The existing extrinsic spherical differential expression commutes with reflection: L_S(f∘A)(w)=L_Sf(-w). These equalities use the total Mathlib derivative operators. In the classical smooth setting at unit points, they give the familiar reflection symmetry of the spherical generator.

                                    • I is a finite coordinate type with decidable equality, and E is the real Euclidean space with coordinates indexed by I.
                                    • f:E→R and w∈E are arbitrary; the first identity quantifies every direction h∈E. No smoothness, unit-norm or positive-dimension premise is imposed on the total-operator identity.
                                    • The radial correction uses max(|I|−1,0), implemented by natural-number subtraction before conversion to R.

                                    Reflection identities

                                    \[D(f\circ A)(w)[h]=-Df(-w)[h],\qquad \mathcal L_S(f\circ A)(w)=\mathcal L_Sf(-w).\]

                                    Reflection symmetry of the spherical differential expression

                                    Read this first

                                    Mathematical statement

                                    Let A(x)=-x on E=R^I, where I is finite. For every real-valued ambient function f and every w,h∈E, the first derivative of f∘A at w applied to h equals -Df(-w)[h]. The existing extrinsic spherical differential expression commutes with reflection: L_S(f∘A)(w)=L_Sf(-w). These equalities use the total Mathlib derivative operators. In the classical smooth setting at unit points, they give the familiar reflection symmetry of the spherical generator.

                                    \[D(f\circ A)(w)[h]=-Df(-w)[h],\qquad \mathcal L_S(f\circ A)(w)=\mathcal L_Sf(-w).\]
                                    Lean statement · sphere_differential_operators_comp_neg

                                    The exact Lean statement appears in the adjacent initially closed disclosure.

                                    Download module (.lean)
                                    theorem sphere_differential_operators_comp_neg
    {I : Type*} [Fintype I] [DecidableEq I]
    (f : EuclideanSpace ℝ I → ℝ) (w : EuclideanSpace ℝ I) :
    (∀ h : EuclideanSpace ℝ I,
      fderiv ℝ (fun x => f (-x)) w h = -fderiv ℝ f (-w) h) ∧
    sphereLaplacian (fun x => f (-x)) w = sphereLaplacian f (-w)

                                    Exact module and namespace context

                                    This identity lets a spherical generator act on reflected test functions without recomputing its differential terms. The proof transports the first derivative, differentiates once more, and then contracts the second derivative and cancels the radial signs.

                                    Full assumptions and notation

                                    All objects and hypotheses

                                    • I is a finite coordinate type with decidable equality, and E is the real Euclidean space with coordinates indexed by I.
                                    • f:E→R and w∈E are arbitrary; the first identity quantifies every direction h∈E. No smoothness, unit-norm or positive-dimension premise is imposed on the total-operator identity.
                                    • The radial correction uses max(|I|−1,0), implemented by natural-number subtraction before conversion to R.

                                    Notation and interpretation

                                    A

                                    Ambient negation A(x)=-x.

                                    \[A(x)=-x.\]
                                    D and D²

                                    The total Frechet derivative and D(Df), respectively; classical derivatives when the corresponding regularity is available. Df(x) is zero when f is not differentiable at x; D² applies the same total derivative to the function x↦Df(x).

                                    \[D^2f=D(Df).\]
                                    L_S

                                    The existing expression Delta f(w)-D²f(w)[w,w]-max(|I|-1,0) Df(w)[w]. Here Delta is the finite diagonal sum of D² in an orthonormal basis.

                                    \[\mathcal L_Sf(w)=\Delta f(w)-D^2f(w)[w,w]-\max(\lvert I\rvert-1,0)Df(w)[w].\]

                                    Mathematical proof

                                    Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                                    1. Transport the first derivative

                                    Negation is multiplication by the nonzero scalar -1. Mathlib transports the total derivative through this invertible change of variables, including the nondifferentiable cases handled by its total definition.

                                    \[D(f\circ A)(x)=-Df(-x).\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step
                                      have hD (x : EuclideanSpace ℝ I) :
      fderiv ℝ (fun y => f (-y)) x = -fderiv ℝ f (-x) := by
    simpa only [neg_one_smul] using (fderiv_comp_smul (f := f) (x := x) (-1 : ℝ))
                                    2. Differentiate the transported derivative

                                    The first derivative is the function x↦-Df(-x). Applying total derivative transport once more introduces a second minus sign; the two signs cancel. This gives equality of the actual continuous bilinear derivative expressions.

                                    \[D^2(f\circ A)(x)=D^2f(-x).\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step
                                      have hDfun : fderiv ℝ (fun x => f (-x)) = fun x => -fderiv ℝ f (-x) :=
    funext hD
  have hH (x : EuclideanSpace ℝ I) :
      fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ (fun y => f (-y))) x = fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ f) (-x) := by
    rw [hDfun]
    change fderiv ℝ (-(fun y => fderiv ℝ f (-y))) x = _
    rw [fderiv_neg]
    have ht := fderiv_comp_smul (f := fderiv ℝ f) (x := x) (-1 : ℝ)
    simpa only [neg_one_smul, neg_neg] using congrArg (fun L => -L) ht
                                    3. Contract and remove the radial terms

                                    The ambient Laplacian is the finite diagonal sum of the second derivative in an orthonormal basis, so its reflected value agrees. Bilinearity cancels the two signs in the radial Hessian. The sign of the first derivative is absorbed by replacing the radial vector w by -w. Substitute these three identities into the existing sphere expression.

                                    \[\begin{aligned}\Delta(f\circ A)(w)&=\Delta f(-w),\\D^2f(-w)[-w,-w]&=D^2f(-w)[w,w],\\Df(-w)[-w]&=-Df(-w)[w].\end{aligned}\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step
                                      have hLap : (Δ (fun x => f (-x))) w = (Δ f) (-w) := by
    rw [InnerProductSpace.laplacian_eq_iteratedFDeriv_orthonormalBasis _
        (EuclideanSpace.basisFun I ℝ),
      InnerProductSpace.laplacian_eq_iteratedFDeriv_orthonormalBasis _
        (EuclideanSpace.basisFun I ℝ)]
    simp only [iteratedFDeriv_two_apply, Matrix.cons_val_zero, Matrix.cons_val_one, hH]
  constructor
  · intro h
    simpa only [neg_apply] using congrArg (fun L => L h) (hD w)
  · simp only [sphereLaplacian, hLap, hH, hD, neg_apply,
      map_neg, neg_neg]

                                    Samplinglib original sphere geometry and feature-law supplement v1, 2026-10-23 · Complete authored units[0] and its formula proof, pinned source commit 3212f7eb462e2d2237d0a57c6f1f425a82169cff (historical source) · licensed original

                                    Complete source statement and conditions

                                    Let E be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel measurable structure, and let S be its literal unit-norm subtype. The actual angular cost c(u,v)=arccos(inner(u,v)) is jointly continuous and measurable on S×S. For every pair it lies between zero and pi, equals Mathlib's unoriented vector angle, dominates the ambient chord norm, vanishes exactly on the diagonal, and is symmetric. It satisfies the triangle inequality. These are explicit properties of the angular cost; no inherited chord-distance instance is replaced, no path-length geodesic-distance identification or Wasserstein theorem is included, and no sphere nonemptiness or positive dimension is assumed.

                                    • E is a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel measurable structure.
                                    • S is exactly the unit-norm subtype and c(u,v)=arccos(inner(u,v)). Neither positive dimension nor a point of S is assumed.

                                    Angular geometry on the actual unit sphere

                                    \[c(u,v)=\arccos\langle u,v\rangle,\quad 0\le c\le\pi,\quad \|u-v\|\le c(u,v),\quad c(u,w)\le c(u,v)+c(v,w).\]

For every pair it lies between zero and pi, equals Mathlib's unoriented vector angle, dominates the ambient chord norm, vanishes exactly on the diagonal, and is symmetric. It satisfies the triangle inequality. These are explicit properties of the angular cost; no inherited chord-distance instance is replaced, no path-length geodesic-distance identification or Wasserstein theorem is included, and no sphere nonemptiness or positive dimension is assumed.

The actual angular cost c(u,v)=arccos(inner(u,v)) is jointly continuous and measurable on S×S.                                     Download module (.lean)
                                    theorem unit_sphere_angular_cost_properties
    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E] :
    let S := {w : E // ‖w‖ = 1}
    let c : S × S → ℝ := fun z => Real.arccos ⟪z.1.1,z.2.1⟫_ℝ
    Continuous c ∧ Measurable c ∧
      (∀ u v : S, 0 ≤ c (u,v) ∧ c (u,v) ≤ Real.pi ∧
        c (u,v) = InnerProductGeometry.angle u.1 v.1 ∧
        ‖u.1-v.1‖ ≤ c (u,v) ∧
        (c (u,v) = 0 ↔ u = v) ∧ c (u,v) = c (v,u)) ∧
      ∀ u v w : S, c (u,w) ≤ c (u,v)+c (v,w)

                                    Exact module and namespace context

                                    Read the complete mathematical statement and visible assumptions, then expand the numbered formula proof. Exact Lean remains optional and initially folded.

                                    Full assumptions and notation

                                    All objects and hypotheses

                                    • E is a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel measurable structure.
                                    • S is exactly the unit-norm subtype and c(u,v)=arccos(inner(u,v)). Neither positive dimension nor a point of S is assumed.

                                    Mathematical proof

                                    Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                                    1. Identify the angle

                                    Unit norms cancel the denominator in the vector-angle definition, so the literal arccos cost is the existing unoriented angle. Continuity follows from continuous subtype coercions, the inner product and arccos; finite dimension supplies second countability for the measurable product.

                                    \[c(u,v)=\operatorname{angle}(u,v),\qquad c\in C(S\times S;\mathbb R).\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step
                                      have heq (u v : {w : E // ‖w‖ = 1}) :
      Real.arccos ⟪u.1,v.1⟫_ℝ = InnerProductGeometry.angle u.1 v.1 := by
    simp [InnerProductGeometry.angle,u.property,v.property]
  have hc : Continuous (fun z : {w : E // ‖w‖ = 1} × {w : E // ‖w‖ = 1} =>
      Real.arccos ⟪z.1.1,z.2.1⟫_ℝ) := by fun_prop

                                    Literal module excerpt. Local names retain the surrounding theorem context, available with the complete folded theorem; these are proof ingredients, not extra public premises.

                                    2. Compare a chord with its angle

                                    Set θ=c(u,v)=angle(u,v). For unit endpoints, expand the squared chord norm. The half-angle identity and sin squared bounded by its argument squared yield the chord estimate; both norms and the angle are nonnegative.

                                    \[\|u-v\|^2=2-2\cos\theta=4\sin^2(\theta/2)\le\theta^2.\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step
                                    private theorem chord_le_angle
    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    (u v : E) (hu : ‖u‖ = 1) (hv : ‖v‖ = 1) :
    ‖u-v‖ ≤ InnerProductGeometry.angle u v := by
  let θ := InnerProductGeometry.angle u v
  have hθ : 0 ≤ θ := InnerProductGeometry.angle_nonneg u v
  have hc : Real.cos θ = ⟪u,v⟫_ℝ := by
    simpa [θ,hu,hv] using InnerProductGeometry.cos_angle u v
  have heq : ‖u-v‖^2 = 2-2*Real.cos θ := by
    rw [norm_sub_sq_real,hu,hv,hc]
    ring
  have hh := Real.sin_sq_eq_half_sub (θ/2)
  have htwo : 2*(θ/2) = θ := by ring
  rw [htwo] at hh
  have hs := Real.sin_sq_le_sq (x := θ/2)
  change ‖u-v‖ ≤ θ
  nlinarith [norm_nonneg (u-v)]

                                    Literal module excerpt. Local names retain the surrounding theorem context, available with the complete folded theorem; these are proof ingredients, not extra public premises.

                                    3. Separate points and record the range

                                    The principal arccos lies in [0,pi]. A zero cost forces zero chord, hence equal subtype points. Conversely every unit vector is nonzero and has zero angle with itself. Inner-product symmetry supplies cost symmetry.

                                    \[0\le c(u,v)\le\pi,\quad c(u,v)=0\iff u=v,\quad c(u,v)=c(v,u).\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step
                                        refine ⟨Real.arccos_nonneg _,Real.arccos_le_pi _,heq u v,hchord,?_,?_⟩
    · constructor
      · intro hz
        apply Subtype.ext
        apply sub_eq_zero.mp
        apply norm_eq_zero.mp
        exact le_antisymm (by simpa only [hz] using hchord) (norm_nonneg _)
      · rintro rfl
        rw [heq]
        apply InnerProductGeometry.angle_self
        intro hz
        have hh := u.property
        rw [hz,norm_zero] at hh
        norm_num at hh
    · rw [heq,heq,InnerProductGeometry.angle_comm]

                                    Literal module excerpt. Local names retain the surrounding theorem context, available with the complete folded theorem; these are proof ingredients, not extra public premises.

                                    4. Use the vector-angle triangle inequality

                                    Replace each literal cost by its angle expression and apply the existing vector-angle triangle inequality. This is an angular-cost fact; it does not identify an intrinsic path-length metric, particularly on the disconnected two-point sphere.

                                    \[c(u,w)=\operatorname{angle}(u,w)\le\operatorname{angle}(u,v)+\operatorname{angle}(v,w).\]
                                    Corresponding Lean step
                                      · intro u v w
    rw [heq,heq,heq]
    exact InnerProductGeometry.angle_le_angle_add_angle u.1 v.1 w.1

The actual angular cost c(u,v)=arccos(inner(u,v)) is jointly continuous and measurable on S×S. For every pair it lies between zero and pi, equals Mathlib's unoriented vector angle, dominates the ambient chord norm, vanishes exactly on the diagonal, and is symmetric. It satisfies the triangle inequality. These are explicit properties of the angular cost; no inherited chord-distance instance is replaced, no path-length geodesic-distance identification or Wasserstein theorem is included, and no sphere nonemptiness or positive dimension is assumed.The signature preserves the finite-dimensional real/Borel carrier, actual unit-norm subtype and arccos inner-product cost. Continuity, measurability, range, angle/chord relations, separation, symmetry and triangle are conclusions; no probability law or transport object is part of this theorem.sameAmbient derivatives/operator bounds are explicit generic inputs only to the feature-law result; all feature-integrability/residual/cost estimates are derived. Angular geometry supplies properties of the actual cost. No intrinsic-path/manifold/Wasserstein API identification or chosen statistical instance is claimed.

                                    Explicit cost properties only. The inherited subtype distance is still the ambient chord distance; no metric instance is changed.; No intrinsic path-length identity, installed manifold API, Wasserstein theorem or statistical model is certified. In dimension one the two-point sphere has finite angular cost but no internal path between its two points.

                                      Complete source statement and conditions

                                      Let E be a finite-dimensional real inner-product normed space with its Borel measurable structure and H a complete real inner-product normed space. Let F:E→H have actual ambient Frechet derivative D(w):E→H for every w. Assume nonnegative M1,M2, an operator bound norm(D(w))<=M1 on the closed unit ball and an operator-Lipschitz bound norm(D(w)-D(u))<=M2 norm(w-u) there. Fix y in H. On the actual unit-norm subtype S define K(w)=F(w), angular cost c(u,v)=arccos(inner(u,v)), the actual Bochner mean m(mu)=integral K dmu, V_mu(w)=2 inner(m(mu)-y,F(w)), and G_mu(w)=2P_w D(w)^*(m(mu)-y) with the explicit projection P_w z=z−⟨z,w⟩w, which projects onto w-perpendicular when norm(w)=1. Let Q(mu,nu) be the literal extended nonnegative infimum of the quadratic angular cost over all actual couplings. There exist C1,C2>0, independent of probability laws and unit weights, such that for every actual parameter probability K is integrable, V_mu has the displayed ambient gradient 2D(w)^*(m(mu)-y) at every ambient w, and its projected G_mu is tangent and uniformly bounded by C1 at every unit weight. For every two actual parameter probabilities Q is finite and norm(G_mu(w)-G_nu(u))<=C2*(sqrt(Q).toReal+c(w,u)). Feature boundedness, strong measurability, feature Lipschitz control and residual budgets are derived inside the proof rather than assumed; the returned conclusions are feature integrability, actual ambient gradient, tangency/uniform bound, finite transport cost and the joint sensitivity estimate. The constants may depend on the displayed feature/derivative data, E,H and y. This is a generic feature-law theorem, not a concrete Gaussian scalar-data potential, installed manifold-gradient/Wasserstein API or intrinsic path-length theorem.

                                      • E is finite-dimensional real Hilbert with Borel structure; H is a complete real inner-product normed space, with no separability assumption.
                                      • F:E→H has actual full ambient Frechet derivative D(w) at every w. M1,M2≥0 bound the derivative operator norm and its operator Lipschitz increment on the closed unit ball.
                                      • y is fixed. S is the literal unit-norm subtype; m is the actual Bochner integral, c the literal arccos cost, and Q the infimum of angular squared cost over all actual couplings.

                                      Uniform gradients of quadratic feature-law potentials

                                      \[P_wz=z-\langle z,w\rangle w,\quad V_\mu(w)=2\langle m_\mu-y,F(w)\rangle,\quad G_\mu(w)=2P_wD(w)^*(m_\mu-y),\quad \|G_\mu(w)-G_\nu(u)\|\le C_2\bigl(Q(\mu,\nu)^{1/2}+c(w,u)\bigr).\]

                                      theorem quadratic_feature_law_gradient_angular_transport_control
    {E H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]
    [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H] [CompleteSpace H]
    (F : E → H) (D : E → E →L[ℝ] H)
    (hF : ∀ w, HasFDerivAt F (D w) w)
    (M₁ M₂ : ℝ) (hM₁ : 0 ≤ M₁) (hM₂ : 0 ≤ M₂)
    (hBound : ∀ w : E, ‖w‖ ≤ 1 → ‖D w‖ ≤ M₁)
    (hLip : ∀ w u : E, ‖w‖ ≤ 1 → ‖u‖ ≤ 1 → ‖D w-D u‖ ≤ M₂*‖w-u‖)
    (y : H) :
    let S := {w : E // ‖w‖ = 1}
    let K : S → H := fun w => F w.1
    let c : S × S → ℝ := fun z => Real.arccos ⟪z.1.1,z.2.1⟫_ℝ
    let m : Measure S → H := fun μ => ∫ w, K w ∂μ
    let V : Measure S → E → ℝ := fun μ w => 2 * ⟪m μ-y,F w⟫_ℝ
    let G : Measure S → E → E := fun μ w =>
      (2 : ℝ) • ((D w).adjoint (m μ-y) - ⟪(D w).adjoint (m μ-y),w⟫_ℝ • w)
    let Q : Measure S → Measure S → ℝ≥0∞ := fun μ ν =>
      AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.Transport.transportCost
        (fun z => ENNReal.ofReal ((c z)^2)) μ ν
    ∃ C₁ C₂ : ℝ, 0 < C₁ ∧ 0 < C₂ ∧
      (∀ μ : Measure S, IsProbabilityMeasure μ →
        Integrable K μ ∧
        (∀ w : E, HasGradientAt (V μ) ((2 : ℝ) • (D w).adjoint (m μ-y)) w) ∧
        ∀ w : S, ⟪w.1,G μ w.1⟫_ℝ = 0 ∧ ‖G μ w.1‖ ≤ C₁) ∧
      ∀ μ ν : Measure S, IsProbabilityMeasure μ → IsProbabilityMeasure ν →
        Q μ ν ≠ ∞ ∧ ∀ w u : S,
          ‖G μ w.1-G ν u.1‖ ≤
            C₂ * ((Q μ ν ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ)).toReal + c (w,u))

                                      Exact module and namespace context
