Named hypotheses are mathematical premises, not facts established by this declaration. Section parameters are described in the mathematical hypotheses above; the module link retains their exact source context.

                                          Download module (.lean)
                                          theorem sphere_product_weighted_gradient_integration_by_parts
    {n N : ℕ}
    (f rho g : SphereConfiguration n N → ℝ)
    (hf : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 1 f)
    (hrho : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 1 rho)
    (hg : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 2 g) :
    let V : Fin N → SphereConfiguration n N → SphereAmbient n :=
      fun i x => rho x • sphereProductGradient g i x
    Integrable (sphereProductDivergence V) (sphereProductMeasure n N) ∧
    Integrable (fun x => f x * sphereProductDivergence V x)
      (sphereProductMeasure n N) ∧
    Integrable (fun x => rho x *
      ∑ i : Fin N, inner ℝ (sphereProductGradient f i x) (sphereProductGradient g i x))
      (sphereProductMeasure n N) ∧
    (∫ x, sphereProductDivergence V x ∂(sphereProductMeasure n N)) = 0 ∧
    (∫ x, f x * sphereProductDivergence V x ∂(sphereProductMeasure n N)) =
      -(∫ x, rho x *
        ∑ i : Fin N, inner ℝ (sphereProductGradient f i x) (sphereProductGradient g i x)
        ∂(sphereProductMeasure n N))

                                          Exact module and namespace context

                                          This applies the product-sphere identity to a scalar weight times the coordinate gradient of a C² function. Proof strategy: Differentiate the joint radial extension; Recover a jointly C¹ tangent gradient; Construct the weighted tangent field; Substitute into the proved product identity.

                                          Full assumptions and notation

                                          All objects and hypotheses

                                          • \(n,N\in\mathbb N\) are arbitrary, with no positivity restriction. Thus the ambient dimension is \(n+1\); \(n=0\) gives the two-point sphere and \(N=0\) gives a one-point empty product.
                                          • The scalar field is \(\mathbb R\). All norms, inner products, tangent projections and manifold metrics are induced by the Euclidean structure. Regularity means regularity in the usual stereographic sphere charts and their finite product charts.
                                          • The reference measure is exactly \(\mu=\sigma^{\otimes N}\), with \(\sigma=\tau(S)^{-1}\tau\) and \(\tau=\operatorname{vol}_E.\mathrm{toSphere}\). Its finite nonzero mass and probability normalization are proved internally; they are not extra inputs.
                                          • For every \(f,\rho,g:M\to\mathbb R\), assume \(f,\rho\in C^1(M)\) and \(g\in C^2(M)\), jointly in all configuration coordinates.
                                          • The field is defined by \(V_i(x)=\rho(x)\nabla_i g(x)\). Its C¹ regularity and pointwise tangency are derived. No sign, strict positivity, normalization, or density interpretation is assumed for \(\rho\).

                                          Notation and interpretation

                                          \(E,S,M,\mu\)

                                          The ambient space is real Euclidean space; the sphere carries its induced metric and usual stereographic smooth structure. The configuration has one sphere coordinate for each element of \(\operatorname{Fin}N\). The measure is fixed by Euclidean volume, not supplied arbitrarily.

                                          \[E=\mathbb R^{n+1},\quad S=\{z\in E:\|z\|=1\},\quad M=S^{\operatorname{Fin}N},\quad \tau=\operatorname{vol}_E.\mathrm{toSphere},\quad \sigma=\tau(S)^{-1}\tau,\quad\mu=\sigma^{\otimes N}.\]
                                          \(h^{\mathrm r}\)

                                          This is the specified canonical radial extension of a sphere function with values in a real normed space. Its zero value at the origin totalizes the function. Derivatives defining sphere operators are taken at unit vectors, inside the open nonzero region.

                                          \[h^{\mathrm r}(z)=\begin{cases}h(z/\|z\|),&z\ne0,\\0,&z=0.\end{cases}\]
                                          \(P_x,\nabla_S,\operatorname{div}_S\)

                                          The projection is onto the actual tangent hyperplane. The gradient uses the Euclidean Riesz representative of the radial differential. For a tangent C¹ field, the displayed divergence equals the intrinsic divergence: its radial differential agrees with the sphere differential, kills the normal, and has the same trace as the induced tangent endomorphism. This interpretation of divergence requires tangency.

                                          \[P_xv=v-\langle x,v\rangle x,\qquad \nabla_Sh(x)=P_x\nabla_Eh^{\mathrm r}(x),\qquad\operatorname{div}_SW(x)=\operatorname{tr}_E D(W^{\mathrm r})(x).\]
                                          \(\nabla_i f,\operatorname{div}_M V\)

                                          Write \(x[i\leftarrow y]\) for replacement of coordinate \(i\) by \(y\). Differentiate that sphere coordinate while holding every other coordinate fixed. The pairing and divergence are sums, with no factor \(1/N\).

                                          \[\nabla_i f(x)=\nabla_S[y\mapsto f(x[i\leftarrow y])](x_i),\qquad\operatorname{div}_M V(x)=\sum_{i\in\operatorname{Fin}N}\operatorname{div}_S[y\mapsto V_i(x[i\leftarrow y])](x_i).\]
                                          • Each integral uses \(\mu\); all sums run over \(\operatorname{Fin}N\). There is no empirical averaging factor.
                                          • The measure inverse is taken in the nonnegative extended reals. Its finite positive denominator is established before normalization is used.

                                          Mathematical proof

                                          Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                                          1. Differentiate the joint radial extension

                                          Normalize every ambient coordinate on the open set where none is zero. Intrinsic C² regularity of \(g\) gives C² regularity of the joint radial extension there. Its full Fréchet derivative is C¹; composing with the configuration inclusion preserves this regularity. Restriction to the fixed linear insertion \(\iota_i:E\to E^{\operatorname{Fin}N}\) in coordinate \(i\) is the derivative of the sphere section \(g_{i,x}(y)=g(x[i\leftarrow y])\).

                                          \[\widetilde g(z)=g\bigl((z_j/\|z_j\|)_j\bigr),\quad D\widetilde g|_M\in C^1,\quad D(g_{i,x}^{\mathrm r})(x_i)=D\widetilde g(x)\circ\iota_i,\]
                                          Corresponding Lean step
                                          private theorem contMDiff_configurationRadial_fderiv {n N : ℕ}
    (g : SphereConfiguration n N → ℝ)
    (hg : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 2 g) :
    ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N)
      𝓘(ℝ, (Fin N → SphereAmbient n) →L[ℝ] ℝ) 1
      (fun x : SphereConfiguration n N =>
        fderiv ℝ (configurationRadialExtension g) (fun j => (x j : SphereAmbient n))) := by
  intro x
  have hd : ContDiffAt ℝ 1 (fderiv ℝ (configurationRadialExtension g))
      (fun j => (x j : SphereAmbient n)) :=
    (contDiffAt_configurationRadialExtension g hg (fun j => (x j : SphereAmbient n))
      (fun j => ne_zero_of_mem_unit_sphere (x j))).fderiv_right (by norm_num)
  exact hd.contMDiffAt.comp x (contMDiff_sphereConfiguration_coe 1 x)

                                          This is one literal contiguous excerpt from the frozen module. The complete declaration and supporting implementations remain in the folded Lean proof.

                                          2. Recover a jointly C¹ tangent gradient

                                          Apply the fixed real Riesz inverse to the coordinate derivative, obtaining a jointly C¹ ambient vector \(G_i(x)\). The projection \(P_{x_i}\) depends smoothly on \(x_i\) through its explicit inner-product formula. Thus the actual coordinate tangent gradient is C¹ in the complete configuration, not just separately differentiable.

                                          \[G_i(x)=\mathcal R^{-1}\bigl(D\widetilde g(x)\circ\iota_i\bigr),\qquad\nabla_i g(x)=G_i(x)-\langle x_i,G_i(x)\rangle x_i,\qquad\nabla_i g\in C^1(M;E).\]
                                          Corresponding Lean step
                                          private theorem contMDiff_sphereProductGradient {n N : ℕ}
    (g : SphereConfiguration n N → ℝ)
    (hg : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 2 g) (i : Fin N) :
    ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n) 1
      (fun x => sphereProductGradient g i x) := by
  let G : SphereConfiguration n N → SphereAmbient n := fun x =>
    (InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ (SphereAmbient n)).symm
      ((fderiv ℝ (configurationRadialExtension g) (fun j => (x j : SphereAmbient n))).comp
        (coordinateInsertion i))
  have hP : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n →L[ℝ] ℝ) 1
      (fun x : SphereConfiguration n N => (fderiv ℝ (configurationRadialExtension g)
        (fun j => (x j : SphereAmbient n))).comp (coordinateInsertion i)) :=
    (contMDiff_configurationRadial_fderiv g hg).clm_comp contMDiff_const
  have hG : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n) 1 G :=
    (InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ (SphereAmbient n)).symm.toContinuousLinearEquiv.toContinuousLinearMap.contMDiff.comp hP
  have hx : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n) 1
      (fun x : SphereConfiguration n N => (x i : SphereAmbient n)) :=
    contMDiff_pi_space.mp (contMDiff_sphereConfiguration_coe 1) i
  have hi : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 1
      (fun x => inner ℝ (x i : SphereAmbient n) (G x)) :=
    ((innerSL ℝ).contMDiff.comp hx).clm_apply hG
  have heq : (fun x => sphereProductGradient g i x) =
      fun x : SphereConfiguration n N => G x - inner ℝ (x i : SphereAmbient n) (G x) • (x i : SphereAmbient n) := by
    funext x
    unfold sphereProductGradient sphereTangentGradient gradient
    rw [configurationRadialExtension_section_fderiv g (hg.of_le (by norm_num)) x i,
      Submodule.starProjection_orthogonal_val, Submodule.starProjection_singleton]
    simp only [norm_eq_of_mem_sphere, one_pow, RCLike.ofReal_one, div_one]
    rfl
  rw [heq]
  exact hG.sub (hi.smul hx)

                                          This is one literal contiguous excerpt from the frozen module. The complete declaration and supporting implementations remain in the folded Lean proof.

                                          3. Construct the weighted tangent field

                                          Multiply by the supplied C¹ scalar weight. Product regularity gives C¹ components, and orthogonal projection gives tangency at every point. Neither argument uses a sign or a normalization condition on the weight.

                                          \[V_i(x)=\rho(x)\nabla_i g(x),\qquad V_i\in C^1(M;E),\qquad\langle x_i,V_i(x)\rangle=\rho(x)\langle x_i,\nabla_i g(x)\rangle=0.\]
                                          Corresponding Lean step
                                            have hV (i : Fin N) : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n) 1
      (fun x => rho x • sphereProductGradient g i x) :=
    hrho.smul (contMDiff_sphereProductGradient g hg i)
  have hT (x : SphereConfiguration n N) (i : Fin N) :
      inner ℝ (x i : SphereAmbient n) (rho x • sphereProductGradient g i x) = 0 := by
    rw [inner_smul_right]
    have ht : inner ℝ (x i : SphereAmbient n) (sphereProductGradient g i x) = 0 :=
      tangentGradient_tangent (fun y => g (Function.update x i y)) (x i)
    rw [ht, mul_zero]

                                          This is one literal contiguous excerpt from the frozen module. The complete declaration and supporting implementations remain in the folded Lean proof.

                                          4. Substitute into the proved product identity

                                          Apply the preceding finite-product theorem to this actual field. Move the real scalar weight through the inner product and finite sum. This gives the two identities and integrability of each displayed integrand. The preceding theorem and its reviewed supporting lemmas provide the normalization, intrinsic differential identification, annular transport and finite-product steps P1–P4; these are reused proof results, not new premises.

                                          \[\sum_i\langle\nabla_i f,V_i\rangle=\rho\sum_i\langle\nabla_i f,\nabla_i g\rangle,\qquad\int_M\operatorname{div}_M(\rho\nabla g)\,d\mu=0,\qquad\int_Mf\operatorname{div}_M(\rho\nabla g)\,d\mu=-\int_M\rho\sum_i\langle\nabla_i f,\nabla_i g\rangle\,d\mu.\]
                                          Corresponding Lean step
                                            have h := sphere_product_tangential_integration_by_parts f
    (fun i x => rho x • sphereProductGradient g i x) hf hV hT
  simpa only [inner_smul_right, Finset.mul_sum] using h

                                          Download module (.lean)
                                          private theorem contMDiff_sphereProductGradient {n N : ℕ}
    (g : SphereConfiguration n N → ℝ)
    (hg : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 2 g) (i : Fin N) :
    ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n) 1
      (fun x => sphereProductGradient g i x) := by
  let G : SphereConfiguration n N → SphereAmbient n := fun x =>
    (InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ (SphereAmbient n)).symm
      ((fderiv ℝ (configurationRadialExtension g) (fun j => (x j : SphereAmbient n))).comp
        (coordinateInsertion i))
  have hP : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n →L[ℝ] ℝ) 1
      (fun x : SphereConfiguration n N => (fderiv ℝ (configurationRadialExtension g)
        (fun j => (x j : SphereAmbient n))).comp (coordinateInsertion i)) :=
    (contMDiff_configurationRadial_fderiv g hg).clm_comp contMDiff_const
  have hG : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n) 1 G :=
    (InnerProductSpace.toDual ℝ (SphereAmbient n)).symm.toContinuousLinearEquiv.toContinuousLinearMap.contMDiff.comp hP
  have hx : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, SphereAmbient n) 1
      (fun x : SphereConfiguration n N => (x i : SphereAmbient n)) :=
    contMDiff_pi_space.mp (contMDiff_sphereConfiguration_coe 1) i
  have hi : ContMDiff (sphereProductModel n N) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) 1
      (fun x => inner ℝ (x i : SphereAmbient n) (G x)) :=
    ((innerSL ℝ).contMDiff.comp hx).clm_apply hG
  have heq : (fun x => sphereProductGradient g i x) =
      fun x : SphereConfiguration n N => G x - inner ℝ (x i : SphereAmbient n) (G x) • (x i : SphereAmbient n) := by
    funext x
    unfold sphereProductGradient sphereTangentGradient gradient
    rw [configurationRadialExtension_section_fderiv g (hg.of_le (by norm_num)) x i,
      Submodule.starProjection_orthogonal_val, Submodule.starProjection_singleton]
    simp only [norm_eq_of_mem_sphere, one_pow, RCLike.ofReal_one, div_one]
    rfl
  rw [heq]
  exact hG.sub (hi.smul hx)

                                          This is a static integration identity for the specified normalized polar measure and its finite product. It gives no derivative in time, entropy evolution, diffusion existence, or density PDE. Identifying another supplied measure, gradient, divergence, or model generator with these definitions is a separate application obligation. The proof derives the required radial regularity from the intrinsic hypotheses. It neither assumes nor asserts that the totalized radial extension is continuous or differentiable at the origin. All integrals are ordinary finite real integrals. The conclusions include integrability, and no almost-everywhere-in-time or finite-horizon convention is involved. The zero-dimensional sphere and empty product are included. The proof retains the radial factor \(r^n/r\) on positive radii; it does not replace the exponent by truncated natural subtraction. The stated regularity is classical C¹/C². No weak-gradient, Sobolev, nonsmooth-weight, or arbitrary-measure extension is claimed. If \(\rho\) is later called a probability density, its nonnegativity and normalization must be supplied by that application. The present geometric identity does not assert them.

                                          Library supplement: Radial differential divergence

                                          Generic exposition of classical sphere calculus; no primary-textbook completion or novelty claim.

                                          Generic product-sphere calculus supplement, 2026-11-17 · public-support-source.json#support-10 (historical source) · licensed original

                                          Complete source statement and conditions

                                          Write \(E_n=\mathbb R^{n+1}\), \(S_n=\{x\in E_n:\|x\|=1\}\), and \(M_{n,N}=S_n^{\operatorname{Fin}N}\). The dimensions are natural numbers and may be zero. For every natural \(n\), every map \(W:S_n\to E_n\), and every \(x\in S_n\), sum the total scalar derivatives at zero of the coordinate lines \(t\mapsto(W^{\mathrm r}(x+t e_j))_j\), where \(e_j\) is the standard Euclidean coordinate vector. Each total scalar derivative is the ordinary derivative if it exists and zero otherwise. This definition makes no C¹ or tangency assertion. Under intrinsic C¹ regularity the sum equals the ambient Fréchet trace; its ordinary intrinsic vector-field divergence interpretation additionally requires \(W(x)\perp x\) at every sphere point. For a nontangent map it is not asserted to be the divergence of its tangent projection. Here \(W^{\mathrm r}(z)=W(\|z\|^{-1}z)\) for \(z\ne0\) and \(W^{\mathrm r}(0)=0\). Intrinsic C¹ refers to the ordinary stereographic smooth structure on \(S_n\).

                                          • Use the indicated canonical real Euclidean, unit-sphere and finite-product carriers; no positive-dimension restriction is imposed.
                                          • This is a definition or abbreviation. It imposes no unstated regularity, tangency, integrability or probability hypothesis.

                                          Radial differential divergence

                                          \[\operatorname{div}_S^{\mathrm{tot}}W(x)=\sum_{j\in\operatorname{Fin}(n+1)}\operatorname{deriv}_{\mathrm{tot}}\left[t\mapsto(W^{\mathrm r}(x+t e_j))_j\right](0).\]

                                          Library supplement: Actual projected differential gradient

                                          Generic exposition of classical sphere calculus; no primary-textbook completion or novelty claim.

                                          Generic product-sphere calculus supplement, 2026-11-17 · public-support-source.json#support-09 (historical source) · licensed original

                                          Complete source statement and conditions

                                          Write \(E_n=\mathbb R^{n+1}\), \(S_n=\{x\in E_n:\|x\|=1\}\), and \(M_{n,N}=S_n^{\operatorname{Fin}N}\). The dimensions are natural numbers and may be zero. For every natural \(n\), every function \(h:S_n\to\mathbb R\), and every \(x\in S_n\), take the total Fréchet derivative of \(h^{\mathrm r}:E_n\to\mathbb R\), its real Euclidean Riesz representative, and the orthogonal projection to \(x^\perp\). Here the total derivative agrees with the ordinary derivative where it exists and is zero where no Fréchet derivative exists. The definition asserts no regularity of \(h\). Its interpretation as the ordinary intrinsic gradient is asserted only under intrinsic C¹ regularity. Here \(h^{\mathrm r}(z)=h(\|z\|^{-1}z)\) for \(z\ne0\) and \(h^{\mathrm r}(0)=0\); \(\mathcal R^{-1}\) is the inverse real Euclidean Riesz isometry. Intrinsic C¹ refers to the ordinary stereographic smooth structure on \(S_n\).

                                          • Use the indicated canonical real Euclidean, unit-sphere and finite-product carriers; no positive-dimension restriction is imposed.
                                          • This is a definition or abbreviation. It imposes no unstated regularity, tangency, integrability or probability hypothesis.

                                          Actual projected differential gradient

                                          \[\nabla_S^{\mathrm{tot}}h(x)=P_x\mathcal R^{-1}\!\left(D_{\mathrm{tot}}h^{\mathrm r}(x)\right),\qquad P_xv=v-\langle x,v\rangle x.\]

                                          Mathematical proof

                                          Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                                          1. Cancel the finite nonzero total mass

                                          The polar mass is nonzero by the existing polar-measure theorem and finite by the preceding instance. Its extended-real inverse therefore cancels exactly. The proof establishes these facts before normalizing.

                                          Geometric supplement: Induced distance on a round unit sphere

                                          Original exposition of a classical round-sphere distance formula; no claim of novelty or attribution to a primary textbook theorem.

                                          Self-contained geometric supplement, 2026-11-16; expanded exposition of the exact 2026-11-09 contract · units[0], complete statement, definitions and six proof regions in runs/20261116-sphere-distance/source-only.json (historical source) · licensed original

                                          Complete source statement and conditions

                                          Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with \(\dim E=n+1\), where \(n\ge1\), and let \(S=\{z\in E:\|z\|=1\}\). For the literal inclusion \(\iota:S\to E\), give a tangent vector \(v\) at \(z\) the length \(\|D\iota_z(v)\|_E\). Define \(d_S(x,y)\) as the infimum of the lengths of all \(C^1\) paths on the closed unit interval from \(x\) to \(y\), using this induced speed. For every \(x,y\in S\), including coincident and antipodal endpoints, this distance is the angle \(\arccos\langle x,y\rangle\).

                                          • \(E\) has a real inner product and finite dimension \(n+1\); \(n\) is a positive natural number. The rank equality selects the standard \(n\)-dimensional sphere manifold model. Positive sphere dimension is used to find a tangent direction for antipodal endpoints.
                                          • \(S\) is the actual unit sphere in \(E\), and both endpoints are arbitrary points of \(S\). No distinctness or nonantipodality hypothesis is imposed.
                                          • The tangent length is induced by the actual differential of the inclusion into \(E\). It is not a default chart-coordinate norm. The sphere retains its inherited chord metric as a topological subtype; no metric instance is replaced.
                                          • The infimum ranges over \(C^1\) paths on the closed unit interval with the prescribed endpoints. The formal distance is an extended nonnegative real and path length is a lower integral; the equality proves that the value is finite.
                                          • All differentiability and integrability of the constructed paths, and the scalar norm law needed by the path-length API, are proved internally. There is no supplied path, geodesic, derivative bound, length estimate, or additional measure structure among the theorem hypotheses.

                                          Induced distance equals central angle

                                          \[d_S(x,y)=\inf_{\substack{\gamma\in C^1([0,1],S)\\\gamma(0)=x,\ \gamma(1)=y}}\int_0^1\|D\iota_{\gamma(t)}\dot\gamma(t)\|_E\,dt=\arccos\langle x,y\rangle\in[0,\pi].\]

                                          The distance along a round sphere is its central angle

                                          Read this first

                                          Mathematical statement

                                          Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with \(\dim E=n+1\), where \(n\ge1\), and let \(S=\{z\in E:\|z\|=1\}\). For the literal inclusion \(\iota:S\to E\), give a tangent vector \(v\) at \(z\) the length \(\|D\iota_z(v)\|_E\). Define \(d_S(x,y)\) as the infimum of the lengths of all \(C^1\) paths on the closed unit interval from \(x\) to \(y\), using this induced speed. For every \(x,y\in S\), including coincident and antipodal endpoints, this distance is the angle \(\arccos\langle x,y\rangle\).

                                          \[d_S(x,y)=\inf_{\substack{\gamma\in C^1([0,1],S)\\\gamma(0)=x,\ \gamma(1)=y}}\int_0^1\|D\iota_{\gamma(t)}\dot\gamma(t)\|_E\,dt=\arccos\langle x,y\rangle\in[0,\pi].\]

                                          theorem unit_sphere_induced_riemannianEDist_eq_arccos
    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] (n : ℕ) [Fact (Module.finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]
    (hn : 0 < n) (x y : Metric.sphere (0 : E) 1) :
  letI : ∀ z : Metric.sphere (0 : E) 1, ENorm (TangentSpace (𝓡 n) z) :=
    fun z => ⟨fun v =>
      ‖mvfderiv (𝓡 n) ((↑) : Metric.sphere (0 : E) 1 → E) z v‖ₑ⟩
  Manifold.riemannianEDist (𝓡 n) x y =
    ENNReal.ofReal (Real.arccos ⟪(x : E), (y : E)⟫_ℝ)

                                          Full assumptions and notation

                                          All objects and hypotheses

                                          • \(E\) has a real inner product and finite dimension \(n+1\); \(n\) is a positive natural number. The rank equality selects the standard \(n\)-dimensional sphere manifold model. Positive sphere dimension is used to find a tangent direction for antipodal endpoints.
                                          • \(S\) is the actual unit sphere in \(E\), and both endpoints are arbitrary points of \(S\). No distinctness or nonantipodality hypothesis is imposed.
                                          • The tangent length is induced by the actual differential of the inclusion into \(E\). It is not a default chart-coordinate norm. The sphere retains its inherited chord metric as a topological subtype; no metric instance is replaced.
                                          • The infimum ranges over \(C^1\) paths on the closed unit interval with the prescribed endpoints. The formal distance is an extended nonnegative real and path length is a lower integral; the equality proves that the value is finite.
                                          • All differentiability and integrability of the constructed paths, and the scalar norm law needed by the path-length API, are proved internally. There is no supplied path, geodesic, derivative bound, length estimate, or additional measure structure among the theorem hypotheses.

                                          Mathematical proof

                                          Open a step to read its argument and formula.

                                          1. Identify the speed through the actual inclusion

                                          For an admissible sphere path \(\gamma\), write \(f=\iota\circ\gamma\). The manifold chain rule identifies its ambient velocity with the image of the path velocity under the inclusion differential. Thus the induced tangent speed is exactly the ambient speed. Within-interval derivatives give the same value at every interior point; endpoints have zero length measure.

                                          \[f'(t)=D\iota_{\gamma(t)}\dot\gamma(t),\qquad \|\dot\gamma(t)\|_{\mathrm{ind}}=\|f'(t)\|_E.\]
                                          Corresponding Lean step
                                            let inc : sphere (0 : E) 1 → E := Subtype.val
  have hcoe : MDifferentiableAt (𝓡 n) 𝓘(ℝ, E) inc (γ t) :=
    (contMDiff_coe_sphere (n := n) (m := 1) (γ t)).mdifferentiableAt one_ne_zero
  change mvfderiv (𝓡 n) inc (γ t) (mfderiv 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) (𝓡 n) γ t 1) = deriv (inc ∘ γ) t
  calc
    _ = mvfderiv 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) (inc ∘ γ) t 1 := by
      simp only [mvfderiv, mfderiv_comp t hcoe hγ, ContinuousLinearMap.comp_apply]
      rfl
    _ = _ := by
      simp only [mvfderiv, mfderiv_eq_fderiv, ContinuousLinearMap.comp_apply,
        fderiv_apply_one_eq_deriv]
      rfl

                                          2. Control the derivative of the scalar inner product

                                          From the unit-norm constraint \(\|f(t)\|=1\), differentiation gives \(\langle f,f'\rangle=0\). Put \(c(t)=\langle x,f(t)\rangle\). Its derivative is the pairing of \(f'(t)\) with \(x-c(t)f(t)\). Expanding the squared norm of that vector and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives the required estimate. No unit-speed parametrization of the arbitrary path is assumed.

                                          \[c'=\langle x-cf,f'\rangle,\qquad \|x-cf\|^2=1-c^2,\qquad |c'|\le\sqrt{1-c^2}\,\|f'\|.\]
                                          Corresponding Lean step
                                            have horth (t : ℝ) (ht : t ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) : ⟪γ t, v t⟫_ℝ = 0 := by
    have heq : (fun _ : ℝ => (1 : ℝ)) =ᶠ[𝓝 t] (fun s => ‖γ s‖ ^ 2) := by
      filter_upwards [Icc_mem_nhds ht.1 ht.2] with u hu
      simp only [hunit u hu, one_pow]
    have hh := ((hder t ht).norm_sq.congr_of_eventuallyEq heq).unique (hasDerivAt_const t (1 : ℝ))
    linarith
  have hcp_bound (t : ℝ) (ht : t ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) :
      |cp t| ≤ Real.sqrt (1 - (c t)^2) * ‖v t‖ := by
    have hu := hunit t (Ioo_subset_Icc_self ht)
    have hnorm : ‖x - c t • γ t‖ ^ 2 = 1 - (c t)^2 := by
      rw [norm_sub_sq_real, hx, norm_smul, hu, mul_one, Real.norm_eq_abs, sq_abs,
        inner_smul_right, ← show c t = ⟪x, γ t⟫_ℝ from rfl]
      ring
    have hpair : ⟪x - c t • γ t, v t⟫_ℝ = cp t := by
      simp only [inner_sub_left, real_inner_smul_left, horth t ht, mul_zero, sub_zero, cp]
    have hr : Real.sqrt (1 - (c t)^2) = ‖x - c t • γ t‖ := by
      rw [← hnorm, Real.sqrt_sq (norm_nonneg _)]
    rw [hr, ← hpair]
    exact abs_real_inner_le_norm _ _

                                          3. Regularize the angle and pass to the endpoint

                                          Fix \(0<a<1\). The function \(\arccos(a c(t))\) stays away from the derivative singularities at \(\pm1\). Its derivative is bounded above by the speed, because the displayed square-root ratio is at most one. Continuity makes the derivative integrable on the compact interval. Integrate the bound, then pass to \(a=1\) by continuity, using \(c(0)=1\).

                                          \[\frac{d}{dt}\arccos(ac(t))=\frac{-a c'(t)}{\sqrt{1-a^2c(t)^2}}\le\frac{a\sqrt{1-c(t)^2}}{\sqrt{1-a^2c(t)^2}}\|f'(t)\|\le\|f'(t)\|,\qquad \arccos\langle x,y\rangle\le\int_0^1\|f'(t)\|\,dt.\]

                                          4. Choose a great-circle plane, including the degenerate cases

                                          Set \(\theta=\arccos\langle x,y\rangle\) and \(r=y-\langle x,y\rangle x\). The residual is orthogonal to \(x\), with norm \(\sin\theta\). If it is nonzero, normalize it. If it vanishes, choose a unit vector in the orthogonal complement, which has positive dimension. The same endpoint identity holds both for coincident and antipodal points.

                                          \[u\perp x,\quad \|u\|=1,\quad y=\cos\theta\,x+\sin\theta\,u,\qquad 0\le\theta\le\pi.\]

                                          6. Compare the lower integral with every admissible path

                                          For any admissible path, continuous ambient within-interval speed is integrable. The induced lower integral equals the nonnegative embedding of its ordinary speed integral, since the two integrands agree on the interval interior. The lower angle bound therefore applies to every admissible path. Together with the explicit upper arc, this gives equality for the length infimum.

    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    (x : E) (γ : ℝ → E) (hx : ‖x‖ = 1) (hstart : γ 0 = x)
    (hunit : ∀ t ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, ‖γ t‖ = 1)
    (hγ : ContDiffOn ℝ 1 γ (Icc (0 : ℝ) 1)) :
    Real.arccos ⟪x, γ 1⟫_ℝ ≤ ∫ t in (0 : ℝ)..1, ‖derivWithin γ (Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) t‖ := by

  let v : ℝ → E := derivWithin γ I
  let c : ℝ → ℝ := fun t => ⟪x, γ t⟫_ℝ
  let cp : ℝ → ℝ := fun t => ⟪x, v t⟫_ℝ
  have hvc : ContinuousOn v I := hγ.continuousOn_derivWithin (uniqueDiffOn_Icc zero_lt_one) le_rfl
  have hc : ContinuousOn c I := continuousOn_const.inner hγ.continuousOn
  have hcp : ContinuousOn cp I := continuousOn_const.inner hvc

    simpa [c, hx, hunit t ht] using abs_real_inner_le_norm x (γ t)

    have hn : I ∈ 𝓝 t := Icc_mem_nhds ht.1 ht.2

    have hvi : IntervalIntegrable (fun t => ‖v t‖) volume 0 1 :=

  have hcl := closure_minimal (show Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1 ⊆ {a | F a ≤ L} from hFle) hclosed

                                          private theorem unit_circle_frame
    {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] (n : ℕ) [Fact (Module.finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]
    (hn : 0 < n) (x y : sphere (0 : E) 1) :
    let θ := Real.arccos ⟪(x : E), (y : E)⟫_ℝ
    ∃ u : E, ‖u‖ = 1 ∧ ⟪(x : E),u⟫_ℝ = 0 ∧
      Real.cos θ • (x : E) + Real.sin θ • u = (y : E) := by
  let c := ⟪(x : E), (y : E)⟫_ℝ
  let θ := Real.arccos c
  change ∃ u : E, ‖u‖ = 1 ∧ ⟪(x : E),u⟫_ℝ = 0 ∧
    Real.cos θ • (x : E) + Real.sin θ • u = (y : E)
  have hx : ‖(x : E)‖ = 1 := by simpa only [Metric.mem_sphere, dist_zero_right] using x.property
  have hy : ‖(y : E)‖ = 1 := by simpa only [Metric.mem_sphere, dist_zero_right] using y.property
  have hc : |c| ≤ 1 := by simpa [c,hx,hy] using abs_real_inner_le_norm (x : E) (y : E)
  have hcos : Real.cos θ = c := Real.cos_arccos (abs_le.mp hc).1 (abs_le.mp hc).2
  let r : E := (y : E) - c • (x : E)
  have horth : ⟪(x : E),r⟫_ℝ = 0 := by
    simp [r, c, inner_sub_right, inner_smul_right, real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq, hx]
  have hrsq : ‖r‖^2 = 1-c^2 := by
    dsimp only [r]
    rw [norm_sub_sq_real, hy, norm_smul, hx, mul_one, Real.norm_eq_abs, sq_abs,
      inner_smul_right, real_inner_comm (x : E) (y : E)]
    change 1^2 - 2 * (c * c) + c^2 = 1-c^2
    ring
  have hsin : Real.sin θ = ‖r‖ := by
    rw [show θ = Real.arccos c from rfl, Real.sin_arccos, ← hrsq, Real.sqrt_sq (norm_nonneg _)]
  have hsum : c • (x : E) + r = (y : E) := by dsimp [r]; abel
  rw [hcos, hsin]
  by_cases hr : r = 0
  · let B := OrthonormalBasis.fromOrthogonalSpanSingleton (𝕜 := ℝ) n
      (ne_zero_of_mem_unit_sphere x)
    let i : Fin n := ⟨0,hn⟩
    refine ⟨(B i : E), ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
    · exact B.orthonormal.norm_eq_one i
    · exact Submodule.mem_orthogonal_singleton_iff_inner_right.mp (B i).property
    · simpa [hr] using hsum
  · have hrnorm : ‖r‖ ≠ 0 := norm_ne_zero_iff.mpr hr
    refine ⟨‖r‖⁻¹ • r, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
    · rw [norm_smul, Real.norm_eq_abs, abs_inv, abs_of_nonneg (norm_nonneg _),
        inv_mul_cancel₀ hrnorm]
    · rw [inner_smul_right, horth, mul_zero]
    · rw [smul_smul, mul_inv_cancel₀ hrnorm, one_smul]
      exact hsum

                                          Finite-dimensional real inner-product space of dimension n+1 with n>=1.FiniteDimensional R E, n:N, Fact(finrank R E=n+1), and hn:0<n.sameThe rank Fact selects the chart model; positivity is the genuine source condition for arbitrary antipodal endpoint pairs.
                                          Lengths are induced by the differential of the literal sphere inclusion.Local ENorm(v)=enorm(mvfderiv inclusion z v).sameExplicitly retains the induced metric and does not substitute a default tangent-coordinate or chord norm.
                                          Infimum of C1 path lengths, asserted equal to a finite nonnegative real angle.Manifold.riemannianEDist in ENNReal equals ENNReal.ofReal(arccos(inner x y)).sameExtended nonnegative encoding preserves the claimed finite value; smoothness, integrability, and ENormSMulClass are constructed inside the proof.

                                          This identifies the induced length distance of a positive-dimensional unit sphere. It leaves the ambient chord metric unchanged; for antipodal points these two distances are \(2\) and \(\pi\). The condition \(n>0\) is essential for arbitrary endpoint pairs: the two-point sphere has no continuous internal path between its two distinct points. It supplies no global Riemannian bundle instance, general manifold geodesic-existence theorem, transport estimate, stochastic result, or textbook chapter completion. Spherical transport is a possible consumer of the distance identity.
